The strategy view uses 'elimination', which names the test-taking strategies in play, walks the options out one at a time, and ends with the verdict. Both views describe the same question, so a student who is short on content can still reason to the answer. All fields are plain text with no markup, so render 'strategy' in italic with CSS rather than expecting tags. Every chapter and skills section carries an 'exam' field naming the exam it belongs to; meta.exams lists the sections in each. Filter on 'exam' to build a single exam's bank. questionTypes.multiple_choice: one correct option; answer is a string
questionTypes.sata: select all that apply; answer is an array and is scored all or nothing

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate absolutes
optionStrategies.cue: always, never, all, none, only, every
optionStrategies.note: Absolutes are usually wrong because medicine rarely deals in certainties.

optionStrategies.name: Favor qualifiers
optionStrategies.cue: usually, generally, often, may, approximately, most
optionStrategies.note: Qualifiers make a statement realistic. Not automatically right, but worth a second look against an absolute.

optionStrategies.name: Opposite pair, look closely
optionStrategies.cue: increase vs decrease, before vs after
optionStrategies.note: Often one of the pair is correct. Sometimes both are distractors, so treat it as a flag for attention.

optionStrategies.name: Global or umbrella option
optionStrategies.cue: one option covers two or more others
optionStrategies.note: If one option encompasses the others it is often the most complete answer.

optionStrategies.name: Patient-centered option
optionStrategies.cue: asks, involves, or respects the patient
optionStrategies.note: Options that involve the patient beat options that decide for them.

optionStrategies.name: Duplicate facts
optionStrategies.cue: a wrong fact shared by two or more options
optionStrategies.note: One shared wrong fact eliminates several options at once.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
optionStrategies.cue: don't worry, it's nothing, most people are fine
optionStrategies.note: Therapeutic communication reflects feelings and invites more.

optionStrategies.name: Odd man wins
optionStrategies.cue: three options share an idea, one stands apart
optionStrategies.note: When most options point one way, the different one is often correct.

optionStrategies.name: Negative polarity
optionStrategies.cue: avoid, except, not, least, contraindicated, requires further teaching
optionStrategies.note: You are hunting the wrong option. Identify polarity before reading the choices.

optionStrategies.name: Priority key word
optionStrategies.cue: priority, immediate, first, best, most, least
optionStrategies.note: More than one option may be true. The key word decides how to choose among them.

optionStrategies.name: Apply the ABCs
optionStrategies.note: In ordering and priority questions, airway, breathing, and circulation come first, then safety, then comfort.

optionStrategies.name: Assessment before intervention
optionStrategies.cue: assess, check, determine versus administer, apply, notify
optionStrategies.note: When the stem asks what comes first and an assessment option is present, assessment usually precedes action.

optionStrategies.name: Treat each option as true or false
optionStrategies.note: Work each option independently. Partial credit means a wrong selection costs you, so only select what the scenario supports.

questions.stem: Four patients are on a medical unit. Which patient is at greatest risk for a fall within the next hour?

options.text: A patient who received a first dose of an opioid two hours ago and is standing at the bedside reaching into the closet
options.rationale: An opioid is a pain medication that also causes sedation and impairs balance. Ask: has this patient's body changed recently in a way the patient has not yet adjusted to? Yes. The dose is the first one, so no tolerance has developed, and two hours is inside the peak effect window. The patient is also standing unassisted and reaching, which moves the center of gravity outside the base of support. New impairment plus an unassisted high-risk movement is the combination that produces a fall.

options.text: A patient who has used a rolling walker at home for six years and is walking the hallway with it
options.rationale: Baseline function means what a patient could already do before this admission. Ask: is this ability new and untested, or long practiced? Long practiced. Six years with the same device is a rehearsed skill, and the walker is present and in use. This is the patient doing something right, offered as if it were evidence of risk.

options.text: A patient with a long-standing spinal cord injury who transfers from bed to wheelchair with a slide board and no help
options.rationale: A slide board is a transfer device that bridges two surfaces so the patient can shift across without standing. Ask: is the impairment new, and is the technique unpracticed? Neither. Long-standing injury with an independent, established transfer method is stable function. The severity of the diagnosis is not the same as instability.

options.text: A patient with a hemoglobin of 8.1 g/dL who is sitting in a chair with the call light clipped to the gown
options.rationale: Hemoglobin is the oxygen-carrying protein in red blood cells; a low value can cause weakness and dizziness on exertion. Ask: is this patient currently doing something that could produce a fall? No. The patient is seated and has the call light within reach, so the risk is real but not active. This is the most dramatic number in the question, which is exactly why it is offered.

questions.takeaway: Fall risk lives in the gap between what a patient can do and what the patient believes they can do. A limitation that is new and unrehearsed is more dangerous than one that is severe and familiar.
questions.strategy: Three options describe patients doing something they have done many times. One describes a patient whose body changed two hours ago and who is moving unassisted.

strategies: Ask what is new rather than what is worst
Watch for the biggest number

steps.action: Sort each patient into new or familiar
steps.detail: Walker for six years, slide board for years, low hemoglobin while seated. Only the opioid changed today.
Two are stationary or assisted by a device. One is standing and reaching.
A hemoglobin of 8.1 is the most alarming number here and the patient is safely seated.

elimination.verdict: The first opioid dose two hours ago in a patient standing and reaching unassisted.

questions.stem: A patient is assessed at high risk for falls because of generalized weakness after eight days of illness. The patient can stand with the assistance of one person and walk ten feet before needing to rest. Which intervention does the nurse add to the plan of care?

options.text: Place the patient on bed rest and provide a bedside commode
options.rationale: Bed rest means restricting the patient to bed. Ask: what happens to the risk factor under this intervention? It worsens. Disuse reduces muscle strength further, so a patient who tolerates ten feet today tolerates less next week. The fall is postponed and made more likely, not prevented.

options.text: Assist the patient to walk a short distance three times daily and increase the distance as tolerated
options.rationale: Progressive ambulation means walking a set distance with help and extending it as strength returns. Ask: does this reduce the risk factor itself, or only work around it? It reduces it. The risk factor is weakness, and weakness is reversed by use. The patient already tolerates ten feet with one-person assistance, so a graded plan is safe and matched to current functional status.

options.text: Instruct the patient to remain in bed and to call before getting up
options.rationale: An instruction is information given to the patient; an intervention is something that changes the situation. Ask: does this change anything if the patient forgets, or needs the bathroom urgently, or does not want to bother anyone? No. Telling a weak patient not to move is a request, and it leaves the weakness untreated.

options.text: Request a bedside sitter to remind the patient to stay in bed
options.rationale: A sitter provides continuous observation, which is a genuine restraint alternative. Ask: what is the sitter being asked to do here? Remind the patient to stay in bed. That spends a scarce resource on enforcing immobility, and the weakness is still untreated. Observation helps when it supports movement, not when it prevents it.

questions.takeaway: Fall prevention is not immobility. Restriction produces the weakness that produces the next fall, so the plan should make movement safer rather than rarer.
questions.strategy: Three options reduce how much the patient moves, one of them using a resource that sounds generous. Only one does anything about why the patient is unsteady.

strategies: Ask whether the option treats the risk or avoids it
Eliminate options that only restrict

steps.detail: Weakness from eight days of illness.
Bed rest, an instruction, and a sitter posted to keep the patient in bed all leave weakness untouched or make it worse.

steps.action: Check the option against current function
steps.detail: Ten feet with one-person assistance is a starting point a graded plan can build on.

elimination.verdict: Assisted ambulation three times daily, increased as tolerated.

questions.stem: A nurse enters a room and finds a patient sitting on the floor next to the bed. The patient is awake and says, 'I slipped getting up.' Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Help the patient back into bed
options.rationale: Moving a patient means changing position before the extent of injury is known. Ask: has an injury assessment been done? No. Lifting a patient with an undetected hip fracture or spinal injury converts a fall into a far worse injury. This is the right action in the wrong order.

options.text: Leave the room to get a lift and two more staff members
options.rationale: Leaving means the patient is unsupervised on the floor. Ask: can help be obtained without leaving? Yes, through the call light or by calling out. The equipment will be needed, and going to fetch it abandons the patient at the moment they are least safe.

options.text: Call for assistance and stay with the patient
options.rationale: Calling for assistance means summoning help without leaving the room, by call light, alarm, or voice. Ask: does this keep the patient supervised while help is brought? Yes. A patient on the floor may have an injury that is not visible and may try to get up alone. Staying is what prevents a second event while help arrives.

options.text: Complete an occurrence report
options.rationale: An occurrence report is the internal safety report filed after an event. Ask: does filling it out change anything about the patient on the floor? No. Documentation follows care, and choosing paperwork over a patient is the classic form of recording a problem in place of addressing it.

questions.takeaway: The post-fall sequence is call for assistance, stay with the patient, assess for injury, notify the provider, follow policy, reassess the plan, then document and file the occurrence report.
questions.strategy: Two options are things that genuinely have to happen. The question is what happens first, and moving the patient before assessing is the inversion this item is built on.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
Sequence the actions that are all eventually correct

steps.action: Ask what could still go wrong right now
steps.detail: An unassessed injury, and a second fall if the patient gets up alone.

steps.action: Remove anything that moves the patient
steps.detail: Lifting before injury assessment risks worsening a fracture.

steps.action: Remove anything that leaves the room
steps.detail: Help can be summoned without abandoning the patient.

elimination.verdict: Call for assistance and stay with the patient.

questions.stem: Which patient meets the criteria for restraint use?

options.text: A patient who wanders into other rooms at night on a unit staffed by two nurses
options.rationale: Staffing describes how many people are available to watch a patient. Ask: is the justification clinical or institutional? Institutional. Wandering is not immediate serious harm, and short staffing is never a reason to restrain. This option is sympathetic and true, which is what makes it tempting.

options.text: A patient with a high fall risk score whose family asks that a vest be used overnight
options.rationale: A fall risk score predicts the likelihood of falling. Ask: does the slide criterion of immediate harm the patient cannot control apply? No. Restraints are specifically prohibited for routine fall prevention, and a family request does not create an indication. Honoring the request feels patient-centered and is not.

options.text: A patient who repeatedly refuses to stay in bed after hip surgery
options.rationale: Refusal means the patient is declining a request. Ask: is the patient unable to control their actions, or choosing differently than the nurse would prefer? Choosing. Getting out of bed after hip surgery is a mobility and supervision problem, not a restraint indication, and restraining a competent patient for noncompliance is punishment.

options.text: A patient in delirium who has twice pulled at the endotracheal tube and continues reaching for it after reorientation, a sedation review, and a family member staying at the bedside
options.rationale: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating confusion with a physical cause. Ask: is harm immediate, and have less restrictive options been tried and failed? Both are yes. An endotracheal tube is the airway, so removing it is immediately life-threatening, and three alternatives have already been attempted without success. That combination is what the criteria require.

questions.takeaway: Two conditions must both be met: immediate harm the patient cannot safely control, and less restrictive options that were tried and were not enough.
questions.strategy: All four patients present a real problem. Only one describes harm that is immediate and alternatives that have already failed.

strategies: Eliminate the institution-as-rationale option
Test both criteria, not one

steps.detail: An airway being pulled out is immediate. Wandering, falling risk, and refusal are not.
Only one option names alternatives that were attempted and failed.
Staffing, fall risk alone, and family preference are all excluded outright.

elimination.verdict: The delirious patient reaching for the endotracheal tube after alternatives failed.

questions.stem: A patient has bilateral soft wrist restraints in place. Which findings require the nurse to intervene? Select all that apply.

options.text: Range of motion has not been performed to either arm during this shift
options.rationale: Range of motion means moving a joint through its normal arc. Ask: is this one of the areas requiring ongoing monitoring during restraint use? Yes. Without it, joints stiffen and the patient loses function that was not lost to the illness.

options.text: The patient has voided 400 mL over the past four hours
options.rationale: Elimination is monitored during restraint use because a restrained patient cannot reach a bathroom. Ask: does this value indicate an unmet need? No. Four hundred milliliters over four hours is adequate output and evidence that the elimination need is being met.

options.text: The patient's spouse is sitting at the bedside reading aloud
options.rationale: Family presence is one of the listed restraint alternatives. Ask: is this a problem to correct? No, it is an intervention already working. It is something going right, offered in a list of things going wrong.

options.text: The patient is calm, fully oriented, and asks to have the restraints removed
options.rationale: The criterion for continuing a restraint is that the behavior threatening immediate harm is still present. Ask: is that behavior still present? No. A calm, oriented patient no longer meets criteria, and the standard is to remove at the earliest possible point rather than at a scheduled time.

options.text: Fingertips are cool and capillary refill is four seconds
options.rationale: Capillary refill is the time for color to return after pressing a nail bed, normally under three seconds. Ask: does this suggest blood is not reaching the hand? Yes. Cool fingertips plus delayed refill together point to compromised circulation distal to the restraint, which is one of the monitored areas and requires immediate release and reassessment.

options.text: The skin under the right wrist restraint is reddened and abraded
options.rationale: An abrasion is a scraped break in the skin surface. Ask: is skin integrity intact? No. Broken skin under a restraint means friction is occurring, which will worsen with every movement until the device is removed or repadded.

questions.takeaway: While restraints are in use you monitor skin integrity, circulation, positioning, range of motion, hydration, elimination, and comfort and mental status. A finding in any of those areas is an action, not an observation.
questions.strategy: Two options describe things going well. Read each finding and ask whether it names a need that is being met or a need that is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Separate findings that are going right from findings that are going wrong

steps.detail: Cool fingers with four-second refill, and broken skin, both demand release.

steps.action: Check what has not been done
steps.detail: No range of motion this shift is an omission in a required area.

steps.action: Ask whether the reason still exists
steps.detail: A calm, oriented patient has lost the indication, so the restraint comes off.

elimination.verdict: Circulation, skin, removal criteria, and range of motion. Adequate output and family presence are fine.

questions.stem: A patient with dementia becomes agitated each evening. Which order, if carried out, would function as a chemical restraint?

options.text: Haloperidol given so the patient will settle and the night shift can manage the rest of the assignment
options.rationale: A chemical restraint is a medication given to control behavior rather than to treat a condition. Ask: what is the stated purpose? Managing the workload. The same drug can be treatment or restraint, and the purpose is the only thing that decides which. Staff convenience is explicitly excluded as a reason to restrain.

options.text: Haloperidol given to treat hallucinations the patient describes as frightening
options.rationale: An antipsychotic given for psychotic symptoms is treating a condition the patient has. Ask: is the drug aimed at a symptom or at the staff's difficulty? At the symptom. This is the near-miss option, and the drug is identical to the keyed answer. Only the purpose differs.

options.text: Acetaminophen given for a headache the patient reports at 1800
options.rationale: Acetaminophen is an analgesic. Ask: is the drug given to control behavior? No, it is given for a reported symptom. Treating pain is also one of the first things to rule out before restraining anyone.

options.text: Melatonin given at 2100 as part of the patient's usual home routine
options.rationale: Continuing a home medication maintains the patient's normal pattern. Ask: is movement or behavior being restricted? No. Preserving a familiar routine is closer to a restraint alternative than to a restraint.

questions.takeaway: What makes a medication a restraint is why it was given, not what it is. Ask whose problem the dose is solving.
questions.strategy: Two options are the same drug at the same time of day. The stem gives you a purpose for each, and the purpose is the entire question.

strategies: Near-miss concept
Eliminate the institution-as-rationale option

steps.detail: Two options use haloperidol, so the drug cannot be the answer.

steps.action: Read the purpose clause in each
steps.detail: One treats frightening hallucinations. One clears the assignment.
Acetaminophen for headache and melatonin for routine both treat the patient.

elimination.verdict: Haloperidol given so the shift can manage the assignment.

questions.stem: A nurse raises all four side rails on the bed of a confused patient who keeps trying to get up. Which statement describes this action?

options.text: It is a universal fall precaution appropriate for every confused patient
options.rationale: Universal fall precautions are the baseline measures given to all patients, such as a low bed, locked brakes, and a reachable call light. Ask: is restricting exit on that list? No. Confusion calls for reorientation and familiar cues, not confinement.

options.text: It is a restraint, because the patient can no longer leave the bed freely
options.rationale: A restraint is any intervention that restricts free movement, including devices that are part of the bed. Ask: can this patient get out of bed? No. The effect on the patient is the same as a device strapped to the body, which is why full rails meet the definition and require the same justification and monitoring.

options.text: It is a safety measure that needs no order, because the rails are part of the bed
options.rationale: Ownership of the equipment does not change its effect. Ask: does the definition of restraint depend on what the device is attached to, or on what it prevents? On what it prevents. This is the belief that makes this the most commonly missed item in the topic.

options.text: It is appropriate as long as the patient's family agrees
options.rationale: Consent addresses whether care happens; criteria address whether it is indicated. Ask: can agreement create an indication that does not exist? No. Family preference does not convert an unjustified restraint into a justified one.

questions.takeaway: Restraint is defined by effect, not by hardware. Four rails up confines the patient, so it carries every restraint requirement.
questions.strategy: Three options argue that this is not really a restraint, using three different reasons. Test each against what the patient can actually do.

strategies: Absolute language and reassurance
Return to the definition

steps.detail: Any movement-restricting intervention counts.
With four rails up the patient cannot leave the bed.
Being part of the bed, being routine, and being agreed to change nothing about the effect.

elimination.verdict: It is a restraint, because free exit has been removed.

questions.nursesNote: 0930: Admitted for community-acquired pneumonia. At home the patient walks to the bathroom without a device. Gets up twice each night to urinate. A diuretic was started this morning. Wears bifocals for reading only. On arrival the bed is in the high position from the transfer and the brakes are locked. The call light is coiled on the bedside table beyond the patient's reach. Personal belongings are in the closet across the room. The patient is wearing hospital socks with tread on both sides. Temperature 38.1 C, respirations 22, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air. The patient asks that the overhead light be turned off and the room kept dark overnight.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that increase this patient's risk for a fall.

segments.text: At home the patient walks to the bathroom without a device
segments.rationale: Baseline function is what the patient could already do before admission. Ask: does this describe a loss? No, it describes intact independent mobility. It is a strength offered among the risks.

segments.text: Gets up twice each night to urinate
segments.rationale: Nocturia means waking at night to urinate. Ask: does this create unplanned movement at the time of day when risk is highest? Yes. Urgency and frequency are intrinsic fall risk factors precisely because they produce hurried trips in the dark.

segments.text: A diuretic was started this morning
segments.rationale: A diuretic increases urine production. Ask: is this new, and does it add to an existing pattern? Both. It will increase the twice-nightly trips the patient already makes, and the patient has no experience of the new frequency.

segments.text: Wears bifocals for reading only
segments.rationale: Bifocals have separate distance and near zones and can distort the view of the floor when worn while walking. Ask: does this patient wear them while walking? No, reading only. The detail is there to be checked, and it rules itself out.

segments.text: The bed is in the high position
segments.rationale: Bed height is an extrinsic fall risk factor. Ask: does it change the distance and angle of a transfer? Yes. A patient sliding off a high bed lands before the feet are under the body, and correcting it takes seconds.

segments.text: The brakes are locked
segments.rationale: Locked brakes keep the bed from rolling during a transfer. Ask: is this a hazard or a universal precaution already met? Already met. It is something going right.

segments.text: The call light is coiled on the bedside table beyond the patient's reach
segments.rationale: A reachable call light is how a patient asks for help instead of getting up alone. Ask: can this patient summon assistance? No. An unreachable call light converts every need into an unassisted attempt.

segments.text: Personal belongings are in the closet across the room
segments.rationale: Keeping possessions within reach is a universal fall precaution. Ask: will the patient cross the room unassisted to get them? Very likely, and that trip is unplanned and unsupervised.

segments.text: Wearing hospital socks with tread on both sides
segments.rationale: Nonslip, well-fitting footwear is a universal precaution. Ask: does tread on both sides provide grip regardless of how the sock rotates? Yes. This is appropriate footwear, not a hazard.

segments.text: Temperature 38.1 C, respirations 22, oxygen saturation 94 percent on room air
segments.rationale: These are the vital signs expected with pneumonia. Ask: do they name a mobility or environmental hazard? No. They are relevant to the illness and contribute nothing to the fall question.

segments.text: Asks that the overhead light be turned off and the room kept dark overnight
segments.rationale: Poor lighting is an extrinsic fall risk factor. Ask: what does darkness combine with here? Nocturia and a new diuretic. A patient making extra unplanned trips in an unfamiliar dark room is the specific combination that produces night falls.

questions.takeaway: Fall risk is assembled from intrinsic factors that travel with the patient and extrinsic factors that belong to the room. The dangerous ones here only matter in combination: nocturia plus a new diuretic plus a dark room plus an unreachable call light.
questions.strategy: Several findings are normal or already correct. Read each one and ask whether it makes unassisted movement more likely, or is simply part of the pneumonia.

strategies: Separate expected findings from hazards
Look for factors that combine

steps.detail: Fever, tachypnea, and a saturation of 94 percent belong to the pneumonia, not the fall.
Locked brakes, tread socks, and reading-only bifocals are precautions met or risks not present.
Two intrinsic factors involving urination, and four features of the room and the plan.

elimination.verdict: Nocturia, the new diuretic, the high bed, the unreachable call light, belongings across the room, and the request for darkness.

questions.stem: Each patient has been assessed as being at risk for falls. For each patient, indicate the intervention that targets the identified risk factor.
columns: Improved lighting and access to eyeglasses
Mobility assistance with transfers and ambulation
Monitor symptoms and adjust medication timing

rows.text: Repeatedly starts for the bathroom the moment the urge is felt and has had two episodes of incontinence on the way
rows.rationale: Urgency means little warning between the urge and the need. Ask: does the intervention get the patient there before the urgency does? Scheduled toileting does exactly that, which removes the hurried unassisted trip rather than forbidding it.

rows.text: Reaches for the arm of the chair, misses it by several inches, and has walked into the bedside table twice
rows.answer: Improved lighting and access to eyeglasses
rows.rationale: Misjudging distance is a spatial perception problem. Ask: is the patient misreading the room or misremembering it? Misreading. Repeated contact with objects that are where they belong points to vision, and lighting and glasses are the targeted fix.

rows.text: Asks what building this is each time someone enters and has twice tried to leave to 'get to work'
rows.rationale: Disorientation means the patient has the wrong model of where and when they are. Ask: is the unsafe movement purposeful within a mistaken belief? Yes. Reorientation and familiar cues correct the belief, which removes the reason for the attempt.

rows.text: Can stand unaided but must stop and hold the handrail after about six feet
rows.answer: Mobility assistance with transfers and ambulation
rows.rationale: Reduced endurance and strength impair balance as the patient tires. Ask: does the intervention build strength while keeping the patient safe? Assisted transfers and ambulation do both, which is why the goal is safe movement rather than rest.

rows.text: Became unsteady on standing within two hours of the first dose of a new antihypertensive given this morning
rows.answer: Monitor symptoms and adjust medication timing
rows.rationale: An antihypertensive lowers blood pressure and can cause unsteadiness on standing. Ask: what is the source of the unsteadiness? A drug effect with a predictable time course. Monitoring symptoms and adjusting when the dose is given addresses the cause rather than the symptom.

rows.text: Has been on bed rest for five days and now needs two people to move from lying to sitting
rows.answer: Mobility assistance with transfers and ambulation
rows.rationale: Deconditioning is loss of strength from disuse. Ask: is this a new weakness produced by restriction? Yes, and the answer to weakness is graded assisted movement. This is the second row in the set with the same intervention, because two different histories produced the same risk factor.

answer.r2: Improved lighting and access to eyeglasses
answer.r4: Mobility assistance with transfers and ambulation
answer.r5: Monitor symptoms and adjust medication timing
answer.r6: Mobility assistance with transfers and ambulation

questions.takeaway: Every patient at risk for falls gets the universal precautions. The individualized plan is built by naming which risk factor is driving this patient's risk and choosing the intervention that targets it.
questions.strategy: Do not assume one intervention per patient. Two rows share an answer, because weakness can arrive by illness or by restriction and is treated the same way either way.

strategies: Match the mechanism, not the diagnosis
Watch for the repeat

steps.action: Ask what the unsafe movement is trying to accomplish
steps.detail: Reaching a bathroom, reaching a chair, reaching a job, or crossing a room on failing legs.

steps.action: Trace each to its risk factor
steps.detail: Urgency, vision, disorientation, weakness, and a drug effect.
Bed rest and illness both produce weakness.

elimination.verdict: Toileting, lighting, reorientation, mobility, medication timing, mobility.

questions.scenario: At 0200 on the third day after abdominal surgery, a patient becomes restless, repeatedly pulls at the nasogastric tube, and tries to swing both legs over the side rail. The last dose of analgesia was given eight hours ago. The patient grimaces when the abdomen is touched and answers questions in single words. Heart rate is 104, blood pressure 148 over 88, temperature 37.1 C, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. The abdomen is soft with bowel sounds present and the nasogastric tube is draining as expected.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Apply soft wrist restraints to protect the nasogastric tube
options.rationale: Restraint is permitted only for immediate harm the patient cannot control, after alternatives have failed. Ask: have alternatives been tried? No. This is the right category of concern acted on before the assessment that should precede it.

options.text: Stay with the patient and secure the nasogastric tube while the analgesic takes effect
options.rationale: Continuous observation is a restraint alternative that protects the device without restricting the patient. Ask: does this keep the tube safe during the interval before the drug works? Yes, and it requires no order and causes no harm.

options.text: Document that the patient is confused and pulling at the tube
options.rationale: Documentation records what was found. Ask: does writing it down change the patient's situation? No. It also mislabels the finding, because the stem describes pain behavior rather than confusion.

options.text: Assess the pain and administer the ordered analgesic
options.rationale: Assessment before intervention means establishing what the problem is before treating it. Ask: does the stem point to a treatable cause of the behavior? Yes. Eight hours without analgesia, grimacing on palpation, and a heart rate and blood pressure elevated by sympathetic response all name unrelieved pain.

options.text: Unrelieved postoperative pain
options.rationale: Unrelieved pain is pain that has outlasted the last dose of analgesia. Ask: do the findings fit? Eight hours since the last dose, grimacing on abdominal palpation, single-word answers, and a heart rate of 104 with a blood pressure of 148 over 88 are the sympathetic response to pain. The pieces fit together only under this heading.

options.text: Nasogastric tube malfunction
options.rationale: Malfunction means the device is not working as intended. Ask: what does the stem say about the tube? It is draining as expected. The finding is there to be checked and it excludes this option.

options.text: Delirium from an undetermined cause
options.rationale: Delirium is acute fluctuating confusion with a physical cause. Ask: is the cause undetermined here? No, the stem hands you one. This is the near-miss, because agitation at night after surgery is often delirium and a patient in pain can look confused.

options.text: Nonadherence to the postoperative plan
options.rationale: Nonadherence means declining to follow agreed treatment. Ask: is this patient choosing, or responding? Responding. Labeling a patient in pain as nonadherent replaces a mechanism with a judgment.

options.text: Whether the patient stops reaching for the nasogastric tube
options.rationale: The behavior was the presenting problem. Ask: if the pain was the cause, what should happen to the pulling once the pain is treated? It should stop. Behavior returning to baseline is the evidence that the hypothesis was right.

options.text: Nasogastric output volume over the next shift
options.rationale: Output volume measures how much the tube is draining. Ask: does it evaluate the pain or the agitation? Neither. The tube was already draining as expected, so this measures something that was never the problem.

options.text: Reported pain rating one hour after the analgesic is given
options.rationale: A pain rating is the patient's own score for pain intensity. Ask: does it measure the thing that was treated? Directly. It is also the measure that does not depend on the nurse's interpretation of behavior.

options.text: Whether a family member is able to stay overnight
options.rationale: Family presence is a useful alternative for confusion and fear. Ask: does its availability measure whether the pain was relieved? No. It is a resource, not an outcome.

questions.takeaway: Agitation is a symptom, so you look for its cause before you restrict the patient. Pain, toileting needs, hunger, thirst, delirium, medication effects, fear, overstimulation, and an unfamiliar environment are the list to work through.
questions.strategy: Two findings that look like background are load-bearing: the eight-hour interval since analgesia and the heart rate and blood pressure. Read them together with the grimacing and the problem names itself.

strategies: Ask why before restricting
Read the values as a group

steps.detail: Eight hours without analgesia, grimacing on palpation, heart rate 104, blood pressure 148 over 88.

steps.action: Rule out what the stem excludes
steps.detail: The tube is draining as expected, and the cause is not undetermined.

steps.action: Match the measures to the treated problem
steps.detail: Pain score and the behavior that brought you into the room.

elimination.verdict: Treat the pain and observe; the problem is unrelieved postoperative pain; evaluate the pain rating and whether the pulling stops.

questions.stem: A patient who managed independently at home has been kept in bed for six days during treatment for an infection. The patient now needs two people to move from lying to sitting. Which statement best explains this change?

options.text: Prolonged rest reduced muscle strength, and the patient is now unable to move safely without help
options.rationale: Deconditioning is the loss of strength and endurance that follows disuse. Ask: is there a cause in the stem that accounts for the loss? Yes, six days of bed rest. Muscle weakens quickly without load, which is why restriction is not a neutral choice and why immobility is itself a fall risk factor.

options.text: The infection has extended and is producing new neurologic weakness
options.rationale: Neurologic weakness comes from damage to nerves or the brain and usually appears in a pattern, such as one side or one limb group. Ask: does the stem describe a pattern? No, it describes global difficulty rising. A spreading infection is a real possibility to rule out, and nothing here points to it.

options.text: The patient has become unmotivated to participate in care
options.rationale: Motivation describes willingness. Ask: does the stem describe refusal, or inability? Inability, and needing two people is a measured functional finding. Substituting a judgment about the patient for a mechanism is how real causes get missed.

options.text: This degree of change is an expected part of aging and will resolve once the patient is home
options.rationale: Expected aging changes develop gradually over years. Ask: does a loss over six days fit that timeline? No. Attributing an acute functional loss to age leaves a reversible problem untreated.

questions.takeaway: Immobility produces the weakness that produces falls. A functional loss that appears over days has a cause you can name and usually reverse.
questions.strategy: Two options offer a label instead of a mechanism. Check the timeline in the stem against the timeline each explanation requires.

strategies: Label instead of mechanism
Match the explanation to the timeline

steps.detail: Six days, from independent to needing two people.
Aging is too slow, and neurologic weakness would show a pattern.
Needing two people is a measurement, not a choice.

elimination.verdict: Six days without load cost the patient the strength to rise.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel tells the nurse that a patient 'looks strong enough to walk to the door alone today.' Which response does the nurse make?

options.text: If the patient seems steady once you are up, it is fine to let go partway
options.rationale: Letting go mid-ambulation is a change in the level of assistance. Ask: who is making that decision, and when? The assistive personnel, in the hallway, based on appearance. Judging readiness is nursing judgment and does not transfer with the task.

options.text: Walk with the patient at the assistance level on the plan, and tell me what you notice
options.rationale: Delegation transfers a task while the nurse keeps the decision and the outcome. Ask: does this response keep the plan intact while using what the assistive personnel observes? Yes. The task proceeds at the specified level, and the observation returns to the nurse, who is the one who may change the plan.

options.text: Leave the patient in bed until I am able to get there myself
options.rationale: Deferring the activity means the patient does not move today. Ask: what does postponing mobility cost? Strength, which is the risk factor the plan exists to treat. This sounds cautious and quietly chooses immobility.

options.text: Document that the patient walked independently today
options.rationale: Documentation records what happened. Ask: has the patient walked yet? No, and independently is not the assistance level on the plan. Recording an outcome that was never observed is both inaccurate and unsafe for whoever reads it next.

questions.takeaway: Assistive personnel may assist with mobility according to the plan. Deciding what the plan should be, and deciding mid-task to change it, stays with the nurse.
questions.strategy: Two options sound safe. One is safe because it keeps the plan; the other is only cautious, and it costs the patient the activity.

strategies: Scope of practice
Ask what each option costs

steps.detail: Deciding the patient is strong enough is an assessment.

steps.action: Keep the plan and the observation
steps.detail: The task is delegated; the report comes back to the nurse.
Leaving the patient in bed treats the weakness by making it worse.

elimination.verdict: Walk at the planned assistance level and report back.

questions.stem: A patient was kept in restraints in bed for two days because of severe agitation during an acute illness. The restraints were removed this morning. Which finding indicates a complication of the restraints rather than a feature of the illness?

options.text: The temperature is 38.0 C
options.rationale: Fever is a systemic response to infection or inflammation. Ask: can a device holding a limb still raise body temperature? No. This belongs to whatever brought the patient in.

options.text: The white blood cell count remains elevated
options.rationale: White blood cells rise in response to infection and inflammation. Ask: is this a local effect of being held still? No. It tracks the underlying illness.

options.text: The patient cannot bear weight to stand and needs two people to pivot to the chair
options.rationale: Loss of mobility is one of the listed complications of restraint. Ask: does the finding match the body parts that were held still and the length of time they were held? Yes, two days immobilized in bed. Muscle strength falls quickly without load, and this is the deficit that was created by the treatment rather than by the disease.

options.text: The patient reports a dry mouth after taking nothing by mouth overnight
options.rationale: Dry mouth follows reduced oral intake. Ask: does the stem already supply a cause? Yes, nothing by mouth overnight. Hydration is a genuine monitoring area during restraint use, and this particular finding is already explained.

questions.takeaway: Restraints cause skin and neurovascular injury, increased agitation and confusion, loss of mobility, and injury sustained trying to escape. Two days held still is enough to cost a patient the strength to stand.
questions.strategy: Three findings could belong to almost any acutely ill patient. Ask which one was produced by being held still.

strategies: Ask what the device could physically cause
Match the finding to the site

steps.action: Ask what the restraint could physically cause
steps.detail: Two days of no weight bearing and no walking.
Unable to bear weight, needing two people to pivot.
Fever, white count, and dry mouth all have other causes in the stem or the illness.

elimination.verdict: Loss of the ability to bear weight after two days held still.

questions.stem: A patient's fall prevention plan lists weakness as the primary risk factor. Which addition to the plan most directly addresses that risk factor?

options.text: A bed alarm set to sound when the patient sits up
options.rationale: A bed alarm signals that movement has already started. Ask: does it make the patient stronger or the movement safer? Neither. It buys seconds and only helps if someone is close enough to respond. It is detection offered in place of prevention.

options.text: Moving the patient to a room closer to the nurses' station
options.rationale: Proximity shortens response time. Ask: does it change why the patient is unsteady? No. It is a reasonable supporting measure and it treats nothing.

options.text: Scheduled toileting every one to two hours
options.rationale: Scheduled toileting prevents hurried trips driven by urgency. Ask: is urgency the named risk factor here? No, weakness is. This is a correct intervention aimed at a different problem, which is the most common way a fall prevention question goes wrong.

options.text: A referral for a strengthening and gait program with progressive ambulation
options.rationale: A strengthening and gait program builds muscle and retrains walking under supervision. Ask: does the intervention change the risk factor, or work around it? It changes it. Weakness is treated by graded use, and the therapist, nurse, and assistive personnel share the work of carrying it out.

questions.takeaway: Match the intervention to the named risk factor. Interventions that detect movement or shorten response time are useful, and they do not treat the deficit.
questions.strategy: Every option appears in real fall prevention plans. The stem names one risk factor, and only one option acts on it.

strategies: Correct action, wrong question
Ask whether the option treats or detects

steps.detail: Weakness.
One treats, two detect or shorten response, one treats a different factor.
Scheduled toileting belongs to urgency and frequency, not to weakness.

elimination.verdict: Referral for a strengthening and gait program.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient who has been on bed rest for five days is getting up for the first time. Before standing, the nurse has the patient sit at the edge of the bed. The patient says the room is 'swimming,' and the heart rate rises from 78 to 106.

The finding that most increases the risk for injury at this moment is [[1]].

The nurse's next action is to [[2]].

The change that would show the plan is working is [[3]].

options.text: the patient's report of boredom during the stay
options.rationale: Boredom describes how the stay has felt. Ask: does it contribute to injury during this transfer? No. It is true and inert.

options.text: the five days of bed rest
options.rationale: Bed rest is the exposure that produced the deconditioning. Ask: is it a finding at this moment, or the history that set the moment up? The history. It explains why the patient is at risk and it is not what would injure the patient in the next thirty seconds. This is the genuine near miss in the pair.

options.text: a two-pound weight loss since admission
options.rationale: A small weight change over a short admission is common and nonspecific. Ask: does it explain dizziness on sitting? No, and it is the kind of measured value that looks meaningful because it has a number attached.

options.text: the dizziness and the rise in heart rate on sitting up
options.rationale: Together these describe the body failing to keep blood pressure stable when the patient changes position. Ask: which finding would produce a fall if the patient stood right now? This one. A rate climbing from 78 to 106 is the heart compensating, and the dizziness is the brain not yet getting enough. Read as a pair they mean the patient is not ready to stand.

options.text: ask assistive personnel to walk the patient while you finish charting
options.rationale: Handing off an activity means transferring it at the assistance level on the plan. Ask: has this patient been cleared to walk? No, the patient is symptomatic on sitting. Delegating an activity the patient is not currently tolerating passes the risk to someone with less authority to stop it.

options.text: assist the patient to stand immediately so the episode passes
options.rationale: Standing raises the head further above the heart. Ask: does that help or worsen a drop in cerebral perfusion? Worsen. This is the moment the patient is most likely to fall.

options.text: keep the patient sitting and supported until the symptoms settle, then recheck before standing
options.rationale: Sitting at the edge of the bed lets the circulation adjust to the upright position in stages. Ask: does this keep the activity going while removing the danger? Yes. It treats the symptom, preserves the mobility plan, and creates a checkpoint before the riskiest part.

options.text: help the patient lie back down and cancel the activity for the day
options.rationale: Canceling returns the patient to bed. Ask: what does another day of rest do to the deconditioning? Worsens it. The symptom needs managing, not the activity abandoning.

options.text: the patient agrees to get up again tomorrow
options.rationale: Agreement is a statement of intent. Ask: does willingness measure tolerance? No. A patient can be entirely willing and still become dizzy on sitting.

options.text: the patient sits and then stands without dizziness and walks the planned distance with the planned assistance
options.rationale: An outcome is a change in the patient, stated in terms of what the patient can do. Ask: does this measure the deficit that was identified? Yes. It names position change without symptoms, and distance with a specified assistance level, both of which can be observed and compared.

options.text: the bed alarm does not sound during the shift
options.rationale: A silent alarm means no unassisted movement was detected. Ask: does that show improved tolerance for activity, or only that the patient stayed put? Only that the patient stayed put, which is the opposite of the goal.

options.text: the family reports the patient seems more cheerful
options.rationale: Mood is worth knowing and is reported by someone else. Ask: does it measure whether the patient can change position and walk safely? No.

questions.takeaway: After a period of restricted movement, getting up is staged. Symptoms on sitting are the checkpoint, and the outcome is stated as what the patient can do, not as what the patient intends or how the patient feels.
questions.strategy: The first blank has a real near miss. The bed rest is the cause of the problem; the dizziness and the heart rate together are the finding that would injure the patient in the next minute. Read the lead-in for 'at this moment.'

strategies: Read two values together
Distinguish the cause from the current finding

steps.detail: Dizziness plus a heart rate from 78 to 106 means the circulation has not caught up.

steps.action: Pick the action that keeps the activity going
steps.detail: Sitting supported treats the symptom without returning the patient to bed.

steps.action: Write the outcome as patient behavior
steps.detail: Position change without symptoms, and a measured distance at a stated assistance level.

elimination.verdict: The dizziness with the rising heart rate; stay sitting and recheck; stands and walks the planned distance without symptoms.

questions.stem: A nurse tests the strength of a patient's right leg. The patient can slide the leg sideways across the mattress but cannot lift it off the bed. Which grade does the nurse document?

options.text: Grade 2
options.rationale: Grade 2 is movement without gravity, meaning the limb moves when the pull of gravity is taken out of the plane of motion. Ask: which direction did this leg move? Sideways along the mattress, where the bed supports the weight. It cannot lift against gravity, so it sits one grade below that.

options.text: Grade 1
options.rationale: Grade 1 is a trace contraction, meaning the muscle flickers under the skin without producing movement at the joint. Ask: did the limb move? Yes, across the mattress. Movement rules this grade out.

options.text: Grade 3
options.rationale: Grade 3 is movement against gravity, meaning the limb can be raised off the surface but holds nothing added. Ask: could this patient lift the leg off the bed? No, and that is exactly the boundary between grade 2 and grade 3.

options.text: Grade 4
options.rationale: Grade 4 is movement against some resistance, meaning the patient lifts the limb and holds it while you press against it. Ask: has this patient passed the earlier step of lifting at all? No. You cannot reach grade 4 without first clearing gravity.

questions.takeaway: Grade 3 is the hinge in the strength scale: it is the grade where the limb just clears gravity. Below 3 the movement only happens in a supported plane, and above 3 you are adding resistance.
questions.strategy: The stem describes movement in one specific direction. Ask whether gravity was opposing that movement or supporting it.

strategies: Locate the movement relative to gravity
Work outward from grade 3

steps.action: Check whether there is movement at all
steps.detail: Yes, so this is above a trace contraction.
Sideways along the mattress means the bed carries the weight.
The leg cannot lift off the bed, so it falls short of grade 3.

elimination.verdict: Grade 2, movement without gravity.

questions.stem: A nurse has just repositioned a patient from supine to a side-lying position. The patient has a nasogastric tube, a urinary catheter, and an intravenous line. Which action does the nurse take next?

options.text: Document the time of the position change and the position used
options.rationale: Documentation records what was done. Ask: does writing it down tell you whether the new position is safe? No. Charting follows the reassessment rather than replacing it, and a problem created by the turn would go unfound.

options.text: Reassess alignment, comfort, pressure areas, skin, tubes and lines, and the ability to breathe comfortably
options.rationale: Reassessment after repositioning checks what the move itself changed. Ask: what can a turn disturb? Body alignment, the tissue now bearing weight, the position of every tube and line, and the mechanics of breathing. With three devices in place, a tube caught under the patient or pulled taut is the predictable harm, and it is found in the minute after the turn or not at all.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees to support breathing
options.rationale: Elevating the head of the bed supports lung expansion and is part of supported Fowler's positioning. Ask: was this the position chosen? No, the patient was placed side-lying. Changing the position again undoes the turn before anyone has checked it.

options.text: Return in two hours to reposition the patient again
options.rationale: Scheduled repositioning limits the time any one area spends under pressure. Ask: is the schedule the next action, or the one after that? The one after. Leaving now means any problem the turn created has two hours to develop.

questions.takeaway: Repositioning is not finished when the patient is moved. Alignment, comfort, pressure areas, skin, tubes and lines, and comfortable breathing are all reassessed afterward, because the turn is what put them at risk.
questions.strategy: Three options are things that genuinely happen around a position change. The stem names three devices, which is the detail telling you what the turn could have disturbed.

strategies: Ask what the action just changed
Assessment before documentation

steps.detail: A nasogastric tube, a catheter, and an intravenous line.

steps.action: Ask what a turn does to those
steps.detail: Displaces, kinks, or traps them under the patient.
Charting and the next turn both follow the check.

elimination.verdict: Reassess alignment, skin, tubes and lines, and breathing.

questions.stem: A critically ill patient with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome remains hypoxemic despite mechanical ventilation. The team plans to place the patient face down with the head turned to one side. Which statement explains this intervention?

options.text: It is a comfort measure that reduces pressure on the sacrum during long periods of bed rest
options.rationale: Turning a patient does relieve pressure on whatever area was bearing weight. Ask: is pressure relief the reason for this particular position in this particular patient? No. Prone positioning is a respiratory intervention here, and treating it as a skin measure misses why the team is doing it.

options.text: It prevents contractures by holding the hips and shoulders in extension
options.rationale: Positioning does prevent contractures by carrying joints out of a fixed posture. Ask: is contracture prevention the reason for proning a hypoxemic patient? No. It is a genuine goal of positioning in general and not the indication in this stem.

options.text: It is first-line therapy for severe acute respiratory distress syndrome
options.rationale: Prone positioning means lying on the stomach with the head facing left or right. Ask: what is the stated indication? It is first-line therapy for patients who are critically ill with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome, which is precisely the condition and severity described.

options.text: It allows easier access to the airway for suctioning and tube care
options.rationale: Access to the airway is a practical consideration during any position change. Ask: does lying face down make the airway more accessible or less? Less, which is one of the reasons proning requires a trained team.

questions.takeaway: Prone positioning is a treatment for the lungs, not a comfort or skin measure. Its stated indication is first-line therapy in severe acute respiratory distress syndrome.
questions.strategy: Every option names a real benefit of some position change. Match the option to the condition the stem describes rather than to positioning in general.

strategies: Match the intervention to the stated condition
Correct action, wrong question

steps.detail: Severe acute respiratory distress syndrome with ongoing hypoxemia.

steps.action: Ask which option addresses the lungs
steps.detail: Only one.
Pressure relief, contracture prevention, and airway access apply to positioning broadly.

elimination.verdict: First-line therapy for severe acute respiratory distress syndrome.

questions.stem: A patient has been confined to bed for two weeks. Which findings are consistent with the metabolic and psychosocial effects of immobility? Select all that apply.

options.text: Expressions of boredom and loss of independence
options.rationale: Psychosocial effects are the ways immobility changes how a patient feels and functions socially. Ask: are these named among them? Yes, alongside isolation, anxiety, depression, and altered self-concept. They matter clinically because a patient who has stopped caring stops participating in the activity that would reverse the physical decline.

options.text: Increased metabolic demand with weight gain
options.rationale: Metabolic demand is the energy the body is using. Ask: does immobility raise or lower it? Lowers it. The effect listed is reduced metabolic demand, so this option has the direction reversed.

options.text: Decreased appetite
options.rationale: Appetite is the drive to eat. Ask: is reduced intake a listed metabolic effect? Yes. It compounds the problem, because a patient already in negative nitrogen balance is taking in less of the protein needed to reverse it.

options.text: Improved sleep quality from increased rest
options.rationale: Rest and sleep are not the same thing. Ask: is improved sleep listed among the effects of immobility? No. Patients confined to bed commonly sleep worse, and nothing in the effects of immobility predicts improvement.

options.text: Rising serum calcium with decreased bone density
options.rationale: Altered calcium metabolism is a listed metabolic effect, and bone demineralization is a musculoskeletal one. Ask: where does the calcium go when bone is not being loaded? Into the bloodstream. Bone releases mineral when nothing is stressing it, which is why weight bearing protects bone.

options.text: Loss of lean muscle mass
options.rationale: Lean muscle mass is the protein-containing tissue that does the work of movement. Ask: what happens to protein balance during immobility? The body breaks down more than it takes in, a state called negative nitrogen balance, and the tissue lost is muscle.

questions.takeaway: Immobility reduces metabolic demand while producing negative nitrogen balance, altered calcium metabolism, loss of lean mass, and decreased appetite, alongside boredom, isolation, anxiety, depression, and altered self-concept.
questions.strategy: Two options describe immobility making something better or increasing demand. Check the direction of each change against what disuse actually does.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Check the direction of every change

steps.detail: Four options are metabolic or musculoskeletal, one psychosocial, one about sleep.
Metabolic demand falls, it does not rise.
Nothing about confinement to bed improves sleep.

elimination.verdict: Lost lean mass, decreased appetite, boredom and lost independence, and rising calcium with falling bone density.

questions.nursesNote: 0800: Patient reports a fall at home last month with no injury. Has lived alone since a spouse died two years ago and says most days are spent in a recliner watching television. Reports smoking about a pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years and drinking three to four beers most evenings. Walks to the mailbox and back once a day without a device. Takes a daily calcium and vitamin D supplement. Reports a serving of milk or yogurt on most days. Height has decreased by two inches over the past decade. Grip is symmetrical and strong bilaterally.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that place this patient at risk for further loss of musculoskeletal health.

segments.text: reports a fall at home last month with no injury
segments.rationale: A prior fall is the strongest single predictor of a future fall. Ask: does the absence of injury make it unimportant? No. The event demonstrates that balance or strength already failed once, and the next fall may land differently.

segments.text: most days are spent in a recliner watching television
segments.rationale: Sedentary time is time without load on muscle and bone. Ask: what does promoting musculoskeletal health require? Regular physical activity and weight-bearing exercise. Sitting for most of the day supplies neither, and disuse takes muscle and bone apart.

segments.text: smoking about a pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years
segments.rationale: Tobacco use is named among the things to avoid in order to maintain musculoskeletal health. Ask: how long has this exposure run? Four decades, which is a sustained modifiable risk rather than an incidental one.

segments.text: drinking three to four beers most evenings
segments.rationale: Excessive alcohol is to be limited for musculoskeletal health. Ask: does three to four drinks most evenings meet that description? Yes, it is a daily pattern well above moderate intake, and alcohol also contributes to falls and to poor nutrition.

segments.text: Walks to the mailbox and back once a day without a device
segments.rationale: Independent ambulation without an assistive device is preserved function. Ask: is this a deficit or a strength? A strength, and it is also the only weight-bearing activity described. It is something to build on rather than a risk.

segments.text: Takes a daily calcium and vitamin D supplement
segments.rationale: Appropriate calcium and vitamin D intake is one of the listed measures that promotes musculoskeletal health. Ask: does this describe a gap? No, it describes the patient already doing one of the right things.

segments.text: Reports a serving of milk or yogurt on most days
segments.rationale: Adequate nutrition supports bone and muscle. Ask: is dietary intake of calcium a risk here? No. Combined with the supplement, intake appears adequate.

segments.text: Height has decreased by two inches over the past decade
segments.rationale: Height loss reflects vertebral compression from reduced bone density. Ask: is this an expected age change or a finding that signals one? It signals osteopenia or osteoporosis, which is the aging change most likely to produce a fracture, and it is measurable evidence that bone has already been lost.

segments.text: Grip is symmetrical and strong bilaterally
segments.rationale: Symmetry and strength on bilateral comparison are normal findings. Ask: does this suggest deficit? No. Comparing sides is how you establish that, and both sides are equal and strong.

questions.takeaway: Musculoskeletal health is promoted by regular physical activity, weight-bearing exercise, adequate nutrition, appropriate calcium and vitamin D, avoiding tobacco, and limiting excessive alcohol. Each of those is a place a patient can be losing ground.
questions.strategy: Four of these findings describe the patient doing something right. Read each one and ask whether it is a gap in the list of protective measures or an example of one being met.

strategies: Separate protective findings from risks
Look for measurable evidence of loss

steps.detail: Daily walking, the supplement, dietary calcium, and symmetrical strength.

steps.action: Find the gaps in the protective list
steps.detail: Sedentary time, tobacco, and excessive alcohol.

steps.action: Add the evidence of loss already present
steps.detail: A prior fall and two inches of height over a decade.

elimination.verdict: The fall, the sedentary days, the tobacco, the alcohol, and the height loss.

questions.stem: A nurse is using the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool. The patient sits at the side of the bed unassisted for three minutes, reaches across midline, and shakes the nurse's hand. With both feet flat on the floor and the knees below hip level, the patient straightens each knee and points the toes. When asked to rise, the patient cannot lift the buttocks off the bed. Which mobility level does this patient have?

options.text: Level 3, moderate assist
options.rationale: Level 3 is assigned when the patient fails the stand test, which checks lower-extremity strength for standing. Ask: could this patient lift or hover the buttocks off the bed and hold it for a count of five? No. The patient passed the first two tests and failed the third, which means there is some lower-extremity strength but not enough to progress toward walking.

options.text: Level 4, minimum or standby assist
options.rationale: Level 4 requires passing the walk test, which checks standing balance and gait by having the patient march in place and advance a foot. Ask: did this patient ever stand? No, the assessment stopped before that point. You cannot skip a failed test to reach a higher level.

options.text: Level 2, maximum assist
options.rationale: Level 2 is assigned when the patient fails the stretch and point test, which checks lower-extremity strength and stability. Ask: could this patient straighten each knee and point the toes with the feet on the floor? Yes, on both sides. The second test was passed as well.

options.text: Level 1, total assist
options.rationale: Level 1 is assigned when the patient fails the sit and shake test, which checks trunk strength and seated balance. Ask: could this patient sit unassisted for more than two minutes and reach across midline? Yes, for three minutes, with a midline reach and a handshake. The first test was passed, so Level 1 is ruled out by the stem.

questions.takeaway: The tool is a sequence of four tests, and the level is named by the first test the patient cannot complete. Sit and shake, stretch and point, stand, walk.
questions.strategy: Every level is described in the stem in order. Read for the point where the patient stopped succeeding, and the level is the test that failed.

strategies: Work the sequence in order
Use the stem to rule levels out

steps.detail: Sat three minutes, reached midline, shook hands. Passed.
Extended both knees and pointed the toes. Passed.
Could not lift the buttocks off the bed, which is the stand test.

elimination.verdict: Failed the stand test, so Level 3, moderate assist.

questions.stem: A patient has completed the sitting and lower-extremity portions of the Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool successfully. Before asking the patient to rise toward standing, which factor does the nurse evaluate?

options.text: Whether the patient reached across midline during the earlier step
options.rationale: Reaching across midline demonstrates trunk control and seated balance. Ask: when is that finding used? In the first test, which the stem says was already completed successfully. It is accurate information that has already done its work.

options.text: Whether an assistive device is available at the bedside
options.rationale: An assistive device is equipment such as a walker or cane that supports weight and balance. Ask: is a device required before this step, or permitted during it? Permitted, and used as appropriate. Having one ready is sensible and is not the evaluation specified before this test, which makes this the closest wrong answer.

options.text: The patient's cognition, orientation, and whether delirium is present
options.rationale: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating confusion with a physical cause. Ask: what could go wrong if a patient with adequate leg strength has impaired judgment? The patient stands, misjudges the situation, and falls. Standing is the point where the assessment first puts the patient's weight on their own legs, so mental status is checked before it rather than after.

options.text: The patient's grip strength in both hands
options.rationale: Grip strength measures hand and forearm function. Ask: does grip determine whether a patient can rise from the bed? No. Grip was already sampled during the handshake in the first test, and it says nothing about the legs.

questions.takeaway: Strength and judgment are separate systems and fail separately. A patient whose legs work and whose thinking does not will stand up and go down.
questions.strategy: Three options describe things that are true, available, or already established. Only one names a risk that appears specifically at the moment the patient stands.

strategies: Ask what is new about this step
Discard information already used

steps.action: Name what changes at this test
steps.detail: The patient bears their own weight for the first time.
Impaired cognition, disorientation, or delirium.
Grip and the midline reach belong to the earlier test, and the device is permitted rather than required.

elimination.verdict: Evaluate cognition, orientation, and the presence of delirium.

questions.stem: A patient has left-sided weakness after a stroke. The patient can raise the left arm about halfway toward shoulder height and then cannot lift it any further. Which exercise does the nurse use to maintain shoulder mobility?

options.text: Active-assistive range of motion, with the patient raising the arm as far as possible and the nurse completing the movement
options.rationale: Active-assistive range of motion means the patient moves the joint as far as they can and the nurse supplies the remainder. Ask: does this match what the patient can do? Exactly. The muscle works through the portion the patient controls, which preserves strength, and the joint still reaches full range, which preserves flexibility.

options.text: Active range of motion, with the patient raising the arm through the full arc unaided
options.rationale: Active range of motion means the patient performs the entire movement alone. Ask: can this patient reach the end of the arc without help? No, the stem says the arm stops halfway. The joint would never reach full range, and stiffness would develop in the part that is never used.

options.text: Passive range of motion, with the nurse moving the arm through the whole arc
options.rationale: Passive range of motion means someone else moves the joint while the patient's muscle does nothing. Ask: can this patient contribute any of the movement? Yes, about half of it. Taking over the whole arc wastes the muscle activity the patient still has, and passive work maintains flexibility without building strength.

options.text: Isometric exercise, with the patient tightening the shoulder muscles without moving the joint
options.rationale: Isometric exercise contracts the muscle without moving the joint. Ask: what is the goal in this stem? Maintaining shoulder mobility, which requires movement. Isometric work builds static strength and joint stability and does nothing for range.

questions.takeaway: Whenever a patient can contribute any part of a movement, they do that part. Active-assistive is the choice that keeps muscle working and still carries the joint through full range.
questions.strategy: The stem gives you exactly how much the patient can do. Match the option to that amount rather than to how impaired the patient sounds.

strategies: Match the option to the stated ability
Eliminate the option that does too much for the patient

steps.detail: Raises the arm halfway, then stops.
Full active is beyond the patient; fully passive removes work the patient can still do.
Mobility means range, which rules out an exercise with no joint movement.

elimination.verdict: Active-assistive range of motion.

questions.stem: A patient has a long arm cast after a forearm fracture and will wear it for six weeks. The patient asks how to avoid losing strength in that arm. Which exercise does the nurse teach?

options.text: Lift a light hand weight with the casted arm
options.rationale: Lifting a weight through an arc is isotonic exercise, in which the muscle contracts while the joint moves. Ask: is joint movement possible or desirable here? Neither. This is the correct exercise for building dynamic strength and the wrong one for a limb that must stay still.

options.text: Rest the arm completely until the cast is removed
options.rationale: Complete rest means no muscle activity at all. Ask: what happens to unloaded muscle over six weeks? Atrophy, loss of strength, and reduced endurance. Resting sounds protective and guarantees the outcome the patient asked how to avoid.

options.text: Tighten and release the muscles inside the cast without moving the joints
options.rationale: Isometric exercise contracts the muscle without joint movement. Ask: does this work when the joint cannot move? Yes, which is the specific reason it exists. It increases static strength and builds joint stability, and it can be used safely around painful or healing tissue, so the muscle keeps working for the six weeks the joint cannot.

options.text: Move the elbow and wrist through their full range several times daily
options.rationale: Range of motion carries a joint through its arc. Ask: are those joints available? No, the cast holds them. Joints above and below a cast are exercised where they are free, and the joints inside it are immobilized on purpose while the bone heals.

questions.takeaway: Isometric exercise is the answer when a joint must not move. The muscle can still be loaded, so strength and joint stability survive the period of immobilization.
questions.strategy: Two options require the joint to move and the cast makes that impossible. Of the two that remain, one does nothing at all.

strategies: Ask what the cast permits
Eliminate the option that does nothing

steps.detail: The elbow and wrist are immobilized for six weeks.
Range of motion and lifting a weight both do.
Complete rest produces the atrophy the patient is asking about.

elimination.verdict: Isometric contractions inside the cast.

questions.stem: A patient walks the length of the hallway with a nurse. Which findings indicate that the patient exceeded activity tolerance? Select all that apply.

options.text: Heart rate rises from 78 to 92 during the walk and returns to 80 within two minutes of sitting
options.rationale: Activity tolerance is judged by the response to activity and by the recovery afterward. Ask: is the rise proportionate, and did it resolve? A rise of 14 beats with a return toward baseline in two minutes is the expected response to exertion. This is the body working correctly, not failing.

options.text: Heart rate remains 118 ten minutes after returning to the chair
options.rationale: Recovery is the last item on the list of things to evaluate and the one most often skipped. Ask: has the heart rate come back down? No, not after ten minutes at rest. A sustained elevation says the patient did more than the cardiovascular system could absorb, even if the walk itself looked acceptable.

options.text: The patient becomes light-headed and reaches for the handrail
options.rationale: Dizziness is a listed tolerance parameter and it signals that perfusion to the brain has dropped. Ask: does the finding also carry immediate risk? Yes. A patient who needs the handrail to stay upright is at the point where the activity becomes a fall.

options.text: Respiratory rate rises from 16 to 20 and settles back to 16 after three minutes
options.rationale: Respiratory rate is one of the tolerance parameters. Ask: is this rise large, and did it recover? Neither concerning nor sustained. A modest increase during walking that resolves on sitting is the expected response.

options.text: The patient stops twice and says it is hard to catch a breath
options.rationale: Dyspnea is the subjective sense of not getting enough air. Ask: is this on the list of responses used to evaluate tolerance? Yes, and it is reported by the patient rather than measured, which makes it easy to discount. Having to stop is the functional version of the same finding.

options.text: Oxygen saturation falls from 96 percent to 87 percent during the walk
options.rationale: Oxygen saturation measures how much of the hemoglobin is carrying oxygen. Ask: should walking cause it to fall? No. Oxygenation is one of the listed tolerance parameters, and a drop of nine points into the eighties means demand has outrun the patient's ability to supply it.

questions.takeaway: Activity tolerance is heart rate, respiratory rate, oxygenation, dyspnea, fatigue, pain, dizziness, and the ability to recover afterward. Rises during exertion are expected; what matters is how large they are and whether they resolve.
questions.strategy: Two options describe changes that occurred and then reversed. Read each finding as a pair, the value during the walk and the value afterward, before deciding.

strategies: Read two values together
Separate the expected response from the excessive one

steps.detail: Saturation should not fall at all, and a heart rate of 118 is not a small rise.
Two findings returned toward baseline within minutes; one had not resolved after ten.
Dyspnea and light-headedness are tolerance parameters even though nothing measured them.

elimination.verdict: Falling saturation, dyspnea, light-headedness, and the unrecovered heart rate.

questions.stem: A nurse performs a neurovascular assessment on a patient six hours after surgical repair of an ankle fracture. Which finding does the nurse report to the provider immediately?

options.text: Pain rated 5 of 10 that decreases after the ordered analgesic
