options.rationale: Pain is one of the neurovascular parameters. Ask: what makes postoperative pain concerning? Pain that is severe, escalating, or unrelieved by analgesia. This pain responded to the ordered dose, which is the reassuring version of the finding.

options.text: Capillary refill of four seconds in the toes with new numbness of the foot, compared with two seconds and normal sensation on the other side
options.rationale: Capillary refill is the time for color to return after pressure on the nail bed, normally under three seconds, and numbness is loss of sensation. Ask: are these two findings pointing at the same thing, and is there a comparison? Yes on both counts. Delayed refill plus new numbness on one side, with the opposite side normal, is compromised circulation and nerve supply. Absent or diminished pulses, a cool or pale extremity, new numbness, and sudden loss of movement are all findings to report.

options.text: Moderate swelling at the surgical site
options.rationale: Swelling is fluid accumulating in injured tissue. Ask: is this expected six hours after a surgical repair? Yes. What would concern you is swelling that is rapid or increasing quickly, and the stem describes neither.

options.text: Bruising visible along the lateral ankle
options.rationale: Bruising is blood that has escaped into the tissue from the injury and the surgery. Ask: does it say anything about current blood supply to the foot? No. It is an expected finding after a fracture and its repair.

questions.takeaway: Neurovascular assessment is color, temperature, capillary refill, pulses, sensation, movement, and pain, and it is always compared side to side. Two abnormal findings in the same limb with a normal opposite side is the pattern that gets reported.
questions.strategy: All four findings are real and three of them are expected after this surgery. Look for the finding that has an abnormal value and a normal comparison on the other side.

strategies: Separate expected postoperative findings from red flags
Use the unaffected side as the control

steps.detail: Swelling and bruising both follow a repaired fracture.
Pain that eases with the ordered analgesic is not the alarming version.

steps.action: Compare sides on what is left
steps.detail: Four seconds against two, with new numbness against normal sensation.

elimination.verdict: Delayed refill with new numbness, abnormal against a normal opposite side.

questions.stem: A patient has been immobile in bed for two weeks following a spinal cord injury. The nurse finds that both feet rest with the toes pointed downward and the ankles can no longer be brought to a neutral position. Which complication has developed?

options.text: Muscle atrophy
options.rationale: Atrophy is the shrinking of muscle that is not being used. Ask: what would you see? Reduced muscle bulk and lost strength. This patient almost certainly has atrophy too, and atrophy does not lock a joint in a fixed position, which is what the stem describes.

options.text: Foot drop, which is a plantar flexion contracture
options.rationale: A contracture is the permanent shortening of muscle and tendon that limits joint mobility, and plantar flexion is the toes-pointed position of the ankle. Ask: does the finding describe a joint fixed in one position? Yes, both ankles, unable to return to neutral after two weeks of prolonged positioning. That is foot drop, and it is prevented by maintaining neutral alignment, performing range of motion, and using supportive devices.

options.text: Bone demineralization
options.rationale: Bone demineralization is the loss of mineral from bone that is not being loaded. Ask: how would it appear at the bedside? It would not. It shows on imaging or in calcium studies, not as a joint that will not move.

options.text: Venous stasis
options.rationale: Venous stasis is blood pooling in the legs because the muscle pump has stopped working. Ask: does it change the position of a joint? No. It raises the risk of thrombus formation and presents as swelling or as a clot, not as a rigid ankle.

questions.takeaway: Contractures are permanent shortening, so prevention is the whole intervention. Range of motion, neutral alignment, and supportive devices are scheduled rather than offered when there is time.
questions.strategy: More than one of these complications is probably present in this patient. Choose the one that explains the specific finding described.

strategies: Match the name to the finding, not to the patient
Near-miss concept

steps.detail: Both ankles fixed with the toes pointed, unable to reach neutral.

steps.action: Ask what each option looks like
steps.detail: Only one of them is a joint locked in position.
Atrophy and demineralization are likely present and neither produces this.

elimination.verdict: Foot drop, a plantar flexion contracture.

questions.stem: A patient is on bed rest after spinal surgery. The nurse hears diminished breath sounds at both lung bases with no adventitious sounds, notes that the patient's cough is weak, and finds that the oxygen saturation has fallen from 97 to 92 percent. The temperature is 36.8 C. Which complication is developing?

options.text: Thrombus formation in the legs
options.rationale: A thrombus is a clot forming in a vein where blood has stopped moving. Ask: do any of the findings point to the legs or to circulation? No. Every finding in the stem is respiratory. Thrombus is a genuine risk for this patient and is not what these findings describe.

options.text: Atelectasis
options.rationale: Atelectasis is the collapse of small airways and alveoli that are not being inflated. Ask: do the findings match that mechanism? Directly. Lying flat decreases lung expansion, a weak cough leaves secretions in place, the bases are the dependent regions that collapse first, and the falling saturation is the consequence. Diminished sounds without adventitious sounds means air is not reaching the area rather than moving through something.

options.text: Negative nitrogen balance
options.rationale: Negative nitrogen balance means the body is breaking down more protein than it takes in. Ask: how would it present? As loss of lean muscle mass and poor appetite, found in laboratory values and body composition rather than at the lung bases. It is a metabolic effect of immobility, not a respiratory one.

options.text: Pneumonia
options.rationale: Pneumonia is infection of the lung tissue. Ask: what would the stem show if this were infection? Fever, purulent secretions, or adventitious sounds such as crackles. The temperature is 36.8 C and there are no adventitious sounds. This is the near miss, because retained secretions in a patient who cannot cough do progress to pneumonia. It has not yet.

questions.takeaway: Flat positioning reduces lung expansion, a weak cough leaves secretions in place, and the dependent bases collapse first. Atelectasis is the step before pneumonia, not the same thing.
questions.strategy: Two options are respiratory and one of them requires signs of infection. Check the temperature and the quality of the breath sounds before choosing between them.

strategies: Name the mechanism before choosing
Correct action, wrong question

steps.detail: Diminished bases, weak cough, saturation falling from 97 to 92.
Temperature 36.8 C and no adventitious sounds rules pneumonia out for now.
A leg clot and a protein imbalance do not produce diminished breath sounds.

elimination.verdict: Atelectasis, with pneumonia as the next step if nothing changes.

questions.stem: A patient has been on prolonged bed rest. For each nursing action, indicate the complication of immobility it is intended to prevent.

rows.text: Sits the patient upright and has the patient cough and deep breathe every two hours
rows.rationale: Atelectasis is the collapse of alveoli that are not being inflated. Ask: what does this action change? Lung expansion and the movement of retained secretions, which are the two things that fail when a patient stays flat.

rows.text: Applies sequential compression devices and has the patient perform leg exercises
rows.rationale: Venous stasis is blood pooling in the legs once the muscle pump stops working. Ask: what do compression and leg exercises restore? Movement of blood out of the legs, which is what prevents a clot from forming.

rows.text: Takes every joint through its full arc twice daily
rows.rationale: A contracture is permanent shortening of muscle and tendon that limits joint mobility. Ask: what keeps tissue from shortening? Being carried through its full length regularly. Range of motion is the direct prevention.

rows.text: Repositions the patient on a schedule and lifts rather than drags during the move
rows.rationale: Pressure, friction, and shear are the three mechanical forces that injure skin, and all three reduce circulation to the tissue. Ask: what do the two halves of this action address? The schedule limits time under pressure, and lifting instead of dragging removes friction and shear.

rows.text: Raises the head of the bed in stages and has the patient sit at the edge of the bed before standing
rows.rationale: Orthostatic hypotension is a fall in blood pressure when the patient moves upright, so the brain briefly goes short. Ask: what does staging the position change buy? Time for the circulation to adjust before the patient takes weight, which is why gradual position changes are the listed prevention.

rows.text: Positions a supportive device against the soles of the feet to hold the ankles in neutral alignment
rows.rationale: Foot drop is a plantar flexion contracture, the ankle setting with the toes pointed. Ask: what does holding the ankle at neutral prevent? The shortening that fixes it in that position. This is the second action in the set aimed at contracture, because two different measures prevent the same complication.

questions.takeaway: Immobility damages seven systems through three mechanisms: stasis of fluids, pressure on tissue, and disuse of muscle, bone, and joint. Name the mechanism and the matching intervention follows.
questions.strategy: Do not assume one action per complication. Two rows prevent the same thing, because range of motion and neutral positioning both act on shortening tissue.

strategies: Name the mechanism behind each action
Watch for the repeat

steps.detail: Air moving, blood moving, tissue lengthening, pressure lifting, or circulation catching up.

steps.action: Map that to the failure it prevents
steps.detail: Collapsed alveoli, clot, shortened tissue, injured skin, a drop in pressure on standing.
Full-arc movement and neutral ankle positioning both prevent shortening.

elimination.verdict: Atelectasis, thrombus, contracture, pressure injury, orthostatic hypotension, contracture.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient reports knee pain and instability after a twisting injury. The knee is swollen and the patient cannot fully straighten it.

The study that will show whether a bone is broken is [[1]].

The imaging is clear, but the pain and the instability continue. The study best able to show a torn ligament is [[2]].

A fracture is still suspected even though the imaging looked normal. The study that may reveal it is [[3]].

options.text: an x-ray
options.rationale: An x-ray passes radiation through tissue and shows dense structures clearly. Ask: what is it used to find? Fractures, dislocations, alignment, and degenerative changes. It is the first study for a possible broken bone because it answers that question quickly.

options.text: a computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Computed tomography builds cross-sectional images and gives more detail of bone than a plain film. Ask: is more detail needed before anyone knows whether a bone is broken? No. It earns its place with complex fractures, once a fracture is known or strongly suspected.

options.text: an ultrasound
options.rationale: Ultrasound uses sound waves and can assess tendons, muscles, fluid collections, and some joint abnormalities. Ask: does it see through and into bone? No. Bone reflects the sound, so it is not the study for a suspected fracture.

options.text: magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging shows soft tissue best. Ask: is the question in this sentence about soft tissue? No, it is about bone. This is the right study for a different question in the same knee.

options.text: a computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Computed tomography is the detailed bone study. Ask: is a ligament bone? No, it is soft tissue connecting bone to bone. This is the near miss, because both this and the correct answer are cross-sectional and both sound like more information than an x-ray.

options.text: a bone scan
options.rationale: A bone scan detects areas of increased bone activity, such as occult fractures, infection, or tumors. Ask: is the concern here bone activity or torn tissue? Torn tissue. A ligament tear does not light up a bone scan.

options.text: magnetic resonance imaging
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is best for soft tissue, including muscles, ligaments, tendons, cartilage, spinal structures, and bone marrow. Ask: what is a ligament? Soft tissue connecting bone to bone, and this is the study that shows it. Persistent instability with clear plain imaging points at ligament rather than bone.

options.text: a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan
options.rationale: This scan measures bone mineral density and is used to assess osteoporosis. Ask: does it evaluate an acute injury? No. It answers a question about how strong bone is over time, not what tore today.

options.text: a bone scan
options.rationale: A bone scan detects areas of increased bone activity, and healing or injured bone is metabolically active. Ask: what is it specifically described as finding? Occult fractures, infection, tumors, and areas of increased bone activity. Occult means present but not visible on ordinary imaging, which is exactly the situation in this sentence.

options.text: a dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry scan
options.rationale: This scan measures bone mineral density. Ask: does it locate a break? No. It reports how dense the bone is, which is a different question from whether this bone is cracked.

options.text: a computed tomography scan
options.rationale: Computed tomography provides more detailed bone images and is useful for complex fractures. Ask: what is it best used for, mapping a known fracture or finding one nothing else has shown? Mapping. This is the strongest distractor, because more detail sounds like the way to find something that is hiding.

options.text: an ultrasound
options.rationale: Ultrasound assesses tendons, muscles, fluid collections, and some joint abnormalities. Ask: can it find a fracture hidden inside bone? No, sound does not penetrate bone well enough to answer that.

questions.takeaway: Match the study to the tissue and to the question. X-ray for a suspected break, computed tomography for detail on bone, magnetic resonance imaging for soft tissue, bone scan for a fracture nothing else has shown, and dual-energy absorptiometry for density.
questions.strategy: The second and third sentences both offer computed tomography, and it is wrong both times for different reasons. Ask what tissue the sentence is about, then whether the fracture is being found or being mapped.

strategies: Match the study to the tissue
Read what each sentence is actually asking

steps.detail: Bone questions go to plain film, computed tomography, or bone scan. Ligament is soft tissue.
First look, more detail on something known, or finding what is hidden.
Bone mineral density answers a chronic question and never an acute one.

elimination.verdict: X-ray first, magnetic resonance imaging for the ligament, bone scan for the occult fracture.

questions.stem: A patient with cerebral edema after a closed head injury has a serum sodium of 118 mEq/L and is becoming drowsy. Which IV solution does the nurse anticipate?

options.text: 3% sodium chloride
options.rationale: A hypertonic solution has a higher osmolarity than plasma, so it pulls water out of cells and into the bloodstream. Ask: does this patient need water moved out of the brain cells? Yes. Severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema are both listed indications for hypertonic saline, and pulling water into the vasculature lowers intracranial pressure while raising the sodium.

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride
options.rationale: An isotonic solution matches plasma osmolarity, so there is no net water movement across cell membranes. Ask: will it shift water out of brain cells or raise a sodium of 118? Neither. It expands volume, which is a different problem from the one in the stem.

options.text: 5% dextrose in water
options.rationale: D5W is isotonic in the bag and becomes hypotonic once the dextrose is metabolized, leaving free water. Ask: what happens to free water in a patient with cerebral edema? It moves into cells. This is among the worst choices here despite appearing on the isotonic list.

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: A hypotonic solution is more dilute than plasma, so water shifts into cells and they swell. Ask: what would that do to a swollen brain? Make it worse. Hypotonic fluids are explicitly contraindicated in increased intracranial pressure, head trauma, and risk of cerebral edema. This is the option that looks right because it is saline.

questions.takeaway: Hypertonic solutions pull water out of cells. That single action is why the same fluid treats severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema at once.
questions.strategy: Three options are saline or dextrose and all four are common fluids. The concentration, not the salt, decides which direction water moves.

strategies: Ask which direction water must move
Watch for the familiar fluid

steps.detail: Water out of brain cells, sodium up.
One hypertonic, one hypotonic, one isotonic, one that becomes hypotonic.

steps.action: Discard anything that adds free water
steps.detail: Half normal saline and D5W both drive water into cells.

elimination.verdict: 3% sodium chloride.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis has completed initial fluid resuscitation with 0.9% sodium chloride and is now hemodynamically stable with a blood pressure of 118 over 70. Which solution does the nurse anticipate for continued maintenance fluid?

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Half normal saline is hypotonic, so water shifts into cells by osmosis and rehydrates them. Ask: which compartment is still depleted once the blood pressure is restored? The cells. Diabetic ketoacidosis after initial resuscitation is a named indication for hypotonic fluid, because the vascular space has been filled and the cellular dehydration remains.

options.text: Lactated Ringer's
options.rationale: Lactated Ringer's is isotonic and produces no net water shift across cell membranes. Ask: what did the initial resuscitation already accomplish? Filling the vascular space, which is what an isotonic fluid does. Continuing it maintains volume without addressing the cellular dehydration that remains.

options.text: 3% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline pulls water out of cells into the vasculature and is reserved for severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema. Ask: does this patient need water drawn out of cells? No. The osmotic diuresis of ketoacidosis has already dehydrated the cells, so pulling more water out would worsen the deficit.

options.text: 10% dextrose in water
options.rationale: D10W is hypertonic and is used for hypoglycemia. Ask: what is the glucose doing in untreated ketoacidosis? It is high. Adding concentrated dextrose at this stage works against the treatment, and dextrose is added later only once glucose falls to a target.

questions.takeaway: Hypotonic fluids move water into cells, which is why they follow rather than lead resuscitation in ketoacidosis. Fill the vascular space first, then rehydrate the cells.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you the blood pressure is already restored. That detail is what moves the answer from an isotonic fluid to a hypotonic one.

strategies: Ask which compartment is still empty
Read what the stem says has already happened

steps.detail: Initial resuscitation is complete and the blood pressure is normal.
Cellular water, lost to osmotic diuresis.
Both would pull more water out of already dehydrated cells.

elimination.verdict: 0.45% sodium chloride.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks why 5% dextrose in water is not used to resuscitate a patient in hemorrhagic shock even though it appears on the isotonic list. Which response is correct?

options.text: It is hypertonic and would pull fluid out of the cells the patient needs to hydrate
options.rationale: Hypertonic solutions have osmolarity above plasma and shrink cells. Ask: where does D5W sit on the classification list? It is listed as isotonic at 252 mOsm/L. This option has the direction and the classification both reversed.

options.text: It is isotonic in the bag, and once the dextrose is metabolized the remaining free water moves into cells
options.rationale: Tonicity describes the solution compared with plasma at the moment of infusion. Ask: does the bag's contents stay the same inside the body? No. The dextrose is taken up and metabolized, leaving water that behaves hypotonically and shifts into cells rather than staying in the vasculature where volume is needed.

options.text: It raises blood glucose, which is the only reason it is avoided in trauma
options.rationale: Dextrose does raise serum glucose, and that matters in some patients. Ask: is the glucose the reason it fails to expand volume? No. The absolute word 'only' also signals a wrong option, because it rules out the actual mechanism.

options.text: It contains too much dextrose and will cause the blood to clot in the tubing
options.rationale: Clotting in the line is a concern with lactated Ringer's during a transfusion because it contains calcium. Ask: does dextrose clot blood? No, it causes red cells to clump and hemolyze, which is why it is never hung with blood. That is a transfusion rule, not the reason it fails as a resuscitation fluid.

questions.takeaway: A solution's tonicity can change once it is in the body. D5W is the standing example, which is why it appears on the isotonic list and is still not a volume expander.
questions.strategy: Two options make a claim about tonicity and they contradict each other. Check which one matches the classification on the solution list.

strategies: Ask what changes after infusion
Absolute language

steps.detail: D5W is isotonic in the bag.
Dextrose is metabolized, leaving free water.
Dextrose and blood is a separate issue from volume expansion.

elimination.verdict: Isotonic in the bag, hypotonic once metabolized.

questions.stem: A patient has lost an estimated 1200 mL of blood during surgery and has a blood pressure of 88 over 52 with a pulse of 118. While blood is being crossmatched, which solution does the nurse expect to infuse?

options.text: 0.45% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Half normal saline is hypotonic, so most of the infused water leaves the vasculature and enters cells. Ask: which compartment is empty here? The vascular space. A fluid that moves water out of that space is the opposite of what is needed.

options.text: Lactated Ringer's
options.rationale: Lactated Ringer's is isotonic at 273 mOsm/L, so infused volume stays in the extracellular space and expands circulating volume without shifting water into or out of cells. Ask: what does hemorrhage empty? The vascular compartment. Volume expansion and hemorrhage resuscitation are the listed uses for isotonic fluids.

options.text: 3% sodium chloride
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline does expand intravascular volume by pulling water out of cells, and it is reserved for severe hyponatremia and cerebral edema. Ask: is there a sodium or a neurologic problem in this stem? No. Using it here treats the volume at the cost of dehydrating cells for no reason.

options.text: 10% dextrose in water
options.rationale: D10W is hypertonic and is used for hypoglycemia and for expanding intravascular volume. Ask: is the problem in this stem a glucose problem? No. It also carries risks of cell dehydration and hypernatremia that are unnecessary when an isotonic fluid will do the job.

questions.takeaway: Hemorrhage empties the vascular compartment, so the fluid that fixes it is the one that stays there. That is the definition of isotonic.
questions.strategy: Two options will raise blood pressure. Ask which one does it without moving water out of cells that are not the problem.

strategies: Ask which compartment is empty
Prefer the fluid with the fewest side effects

steps.detail: Whole blood from the vascular space.

steps.action: Choose the fluid that stays there
steps.detail: Isotonic solutions produce no net shift.
It works, and it dehydrates cells for a problem that is not cellular.

elimination.verdict: Lactated Ringer's.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to transfuse a unit of packed red blood cells. Which actions are required before the infusion begins? Select all that apply.

options.text: Warm the unit to room temperature on the counter for 30 minutes
options.rationale: Packed red cells are stored between 1 and 6 degrees Celsius and must be infused within 4 hours of issue. Ask: does leaving a unit out improve safety? No. It consumes the time window and allows bacterial growth. Blood warming, when indicated, is done with a dedicated device.

options.text: Confirm that signed informed consent is on file
options.rationale: Informed consent is the patient's documented agreement after being told purpose, benefits, risks, and alternatives. Ask: when must it be complete? Before the product is retrieved from the blood bank, because the unit's clock and cold chain start the moment it leaves.

options.text: Have two licensed nurses independently verify the product label against the identification band, ABO and Rh type, unit number, and expiration date
options.rationale: Independent double verification means two qualified people check separately and both sign. Ask: why two people rather than two passes by one? Because one person checking twice repeats the same error. Incompatible transfusion is a sentinel event, and this check is what prevents it.

options.text: Record a full set of baseline vital signs
options.rationale: Baseline vital signs are the values recorded before the infusion starts. Ask: what makes them necessary? Every later reading is judged against them. Temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation are recorded before the unit is started, rechecked at 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes.

options.text: Establish or confirm an 18 to 20 gauge intravenous access
options.rationale: Gauge describes lumen width, and a wider lumen allows red cells through without excessive resistance. Ask: does the size matter for this product? Yes. Eighteen to twenty gauge is the stated requirement for blood, and 18 gauge is preferred for blood products specifically.

options.text: Prime the administration set with 5% dextrose in water
options.rationale: Priming fills the tubing with fluid before connecting it. Ask: which solution may contact blood? Only 0.9% sodium chloride. Dextrose causes red cells to clump and hemolyze, so this action would damage the product being given.

questions.takeaway: The pre-transfusion checks all exist to prevent one event: giving the wrong blood to the wrong patient. Consent, two-nurse verification, adequate access, and baseline vitals.
questions.strategy: Two options describe handling the product itself, and both violate a rule about what may touch blood or how long it may sit.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Separate patient checks from product handling

steps.detail: Consent, identity verification, access, baseline vitals.
Only normal saline may contact blood, and the unit does not sit out.
Eighteen to twenty gauge is required for blood products.

elimination.verdict: Consent, two-nurse verification, 18 to 20 gauge access, and baseline vital signs.

questions.stem: Two nurses are verifying a unit of blood at the bedside. One nurse reads aloud from the blood bank record while the other listens and agrees. Which statement about this process is correct?

options.text: The verification is complete once both nurses sign the transfusion record
options.rationale: Signing documents that verification occurred. Ask: does a signature make the check independent? No. The signature records the process; it does not substitute for it, and both nurses signing a flawed check simply records the flaw twice.

options.text: The process is acceptable if the patient states their own name and date of birth
options.rationale: Patient participation in identification is genuinely good practice and confirms one element. Ask: does it verify the ABO and Rh type, unit number, and expiration date against the label? No. Those are the other required elements, and they are checked against documents rather than against the patient's memory.

options.text: The process is incorrect, because each nurse must verify the information independently
options.rationale: Independent verification means each nurse checks the source documents and the patient separately and then compares conclusions. Ask: did that happen here? No. One nurse read and the other agreed, which is a single check with a witness. The second set of eyes exists to catch the first nurse's error, and it cannot do that if it never looks.

options.text: The process is acceptable as long as one of the two nurses is the nurse who will start the infusion
options.rationale: Which nurse hangs the unit does not change how the check was performed. Ask: does the identity of the infusing nurse make a read-and-agree check independent? No. This adds a true-sounding condition that is irrelevant to the flaw.

questions.takeaway: Two-nurse verification means two independent checks, not one check with a witness. The second nurse exists to catch what the first missed.
questions.strategy: Three options accept the process and add a condition. Ask what the second nurse actually did in the stem before deciding whether any condition rescues it.

strategies: Ask what the second person contributed
Discard conditions that do not touch the flaw

steps.detail: One nurse read aloud and the other agreed.
Nothing the first nurse misread, because the second never looked.
Who hangs it and whether the patient speaks do not make the check independent.

elimination.verdict: Incorrect, because each nurse must verify independently.

questions.stem: A unit of packed red blood cells was started 10 minutes ago. The nurse is planning the monitoring schedule for this transfusion. When does the nurse plan the first reassessment of vital signs after initiation?

options.text: At 60 minutes after the start
options.rationale: Sixty minutes is the outer limit of the ongoing interval once the transfusion is established. Ask: how much blood has entered by then? A substantial part of the unit, which is precisely what the early check is designed to avoid.

options.text: At 15 minutes after the start
options.rationale: Reassessment at 15 minutes is the scheduled early check after a baseline set. Ask: why that early? Because the most dangerous reactions appear in the first small volume, so the check is placed while very little blood has entered. After it, vital signs are taken every 30 to 60 minutes and again at completion.

options.text: At 30 minutes after the start
options.rationale: Every 30 to 60 minutes is the correct interval for the remainder of the transfusion. Ask: is it the interval for the first check? No. This is the right number in the wrong position, which makes it the closest wrong answer.

options.text: At the halfway point of the unit
options.rationale: Monitoring is scheduled by clock time rather than by volume infused. Ask: does the stem or the protocol reference a halfway point? Neither. Rates vary between patients, so a volume-based schedule would place the check at unpredictable times.

questions.takeaway: Baseline, then 15 minutes, then every 30 to 60 minutes, then completion. The 15-minute check exists because early reactions happen in the first small volume.
questions.strategy: Three of these numbers appear in the transfusion protocol. The question is which one belongs to the first check rather than to the ongoing interval.

strategies: Match the number to its position in the sequence
Near-miss concept

steps.detail: Baseline, 15 minutes, every 30 to 60, completion.
Fifteen minutes, before much volume has entered.
Thirty and 60 minutes belong to the phase that follows.

elimination.verdict: Fifteen minutes after the start.

questions.stem: A patient receiving lactated Ringer's through the only IV site is scheduled for a transfusion. Which action does the nurse take before hanging the blood?

options.text: Add 5% dextrose in water to the line to keep it open during the transfusion
options.rationale: Dextrose causes red cells to clump and hemolyze on contact. Ask: may it run alongside or through the same line? No. Only 0.9% sodium chloride may contact blood products.

options.text: Run the blood alongside the lactated Ringer's through a Y connector
options.rationale: A Y connector allows two solutions to meet before entering the vein. Ask: does separating the bags separate the fluids? No, they mix downstream. The incompatibility is with the blood itself, not with the bag it hangs beside.

options.text: Change the solution to 0.9% sodium chloride with new tubing before connecting the blood
options.rationale: Normal saline is the only solution permitted with blood products, and new tubing ensures no residual incompatible fluid remains. Ask: what is the risk being removed? Calcium in the lactated Ringer's clotting the blood in the line. Isotonic saline is also what flushes before and after the unit.

options.text: Flush the existing line with lactated Ringer's and connect the blood to the same tubing
options.rationale: Lactated Ringer's contains calcium. Ask: what does calcium do in the presence of stored blood? It promotes clotting in the line. Flushing with it leaves the incompatible fluid in contact with the product.

questions.takeaway: Only 0.9% sodium chloride touches blood. Dextrose hemolyzes red cells and the calcium in lactated Ringer's clots them.
questions.strategy: Two options keep the existing fluid in play. Ask whether the fluid has to be removed or merely separated.

strategies: Name what is incompatible and why
Ask whether the fix removes the fluid or just moves it

steps.detail: Lactated Ringer's contains calcium.
A Y connector and a flush both leave it in contact.
Normal saline, with new tubing.

elimination.verdict: Change to 0.9% sodium chloride with new tubing.

questions.stem: A patient needs two units of packed red blood cells. The existing peripheral access is a 24 gauge catheter in the dorsal hand. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Use the existing 24 gauge catheter and infuse each unit slowly over 6 hours
options.rationale: Slowing an infusion reduces resistance. Ask: does the time limit permit 6 hours? No. Each unit must be completed within 4 hours of issue because of red cell viability and bacterial growth. This option breaks a second rule to work around the first.

options.text: Establish new access with a 22 gauge catheter in the dorsal hand
options.rationale: Twenty-two gauge is a small-bore size recommended for pediatric, elderly, and fragile veins. Ask: does it meet the stated requirement for blood? No, the requirement is 18 to 20 gauge. Dorsal hand veins are also the sites to avoid in older patients and are a poor choice for a viscous product.

options.text: Establish new access with an 18 gauge catheter in a forearm vein
options.rationale: Gauge describes lumen width, and smaller numbers mean wider lumens. Ask: what does blood require? Eighteen to twenty gauge access, with 18 gauge preferred for blood products because it allows adequate flow without hemolysis or excessive resistance. A 24 gauge catheter is a small-bore size intended for fragile veins and maintenance fluids.

options.text: Use the existing 24 gauge catheter with a pressure bag to overcome the resistance
options.rationale: A pressure bag forces fluid through at a higher driving pressure. Ask: what does forcing red cells through a narrow lumen cause? Hemolysis, which destroys the product being given and releases its contents into the patient.

questions.takeaway: Blood needs 18 to 20 gauge access, with 18 gauge preferred. Working around an inadequate catheter with time or pressure breaks a different rule each time.
questions.strategy: Two options keep the existing catheter and compensate for it. Check each compensation against the rule it would violate.

strategies: Check the requirement first
Test each workaround against a second rule

steps.detail: Eighteen to twenty gauge for blood products.
Six hours exceeds the 4-hour limit; a pressure bag hemolyzes cells.
Twenty-two gauge is still below the requirement.

elimination.verdict: New 18 gauge access in the forearm.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for long-term antibiotic therapy had a left mastectomy with axillary node dissection two years ago and has an arteriovenous fistula in the right forearm for dialysis. Where does the nurse plan vascular access?

options.text: Consultation for a central vascular access device
options.rationale: When both upper extremities are contraindicated and the therapy is long-term, the peripheral options are exhausted rather than merely inconvenient. Ask: what do the selection criteria say? Therapy duration, solution osmolarity, vein condition, and patient diagnosis drive the choice, and therapy beyond a few days already warrants considering a PICC or midline. With a mastectomy limb on one side and a fistula limb on the other, central access is the plan rather than a fallback.

options.text: The left forearm, using the most distal appropriate vein
options.rationale: The affected limb after mastectomy with node dissection has altered lymphatic drainage. Ask: does choosing a distal vein change that? No. The whole limb is avoided, and choosing distal within it applies a correct rule to a site that was already excluded.

options.text: The left external jugular vein
options.rationale: The external jugular is used peripherally in emergencies. Ask: is this an emergency, and is it an appropriate plan for weeks of antibiotics? No on both counts. It also does not address the underlying problem, which is that this patient needs durable access.

options.text: The right forearm, distal to the fistula
options.rationale: An arteriovenous fistula is a surgical connection between an artery and a vein created for dialysis access. Ask: does distance from it make the limb usable? No. The entire extremity with a fistula is avoided, because that limb's circulation is dedicated to dialysis and cannulation threatens it.

questions.takeaway: Contraindicated sites are contraindicated for the whole limb. When both arms are excluded and therapy is long, central access is the plan rather than the last resort.
questions.strategy: Two options try to find a workable spot inside a limb that was already ruled out. Read the exclusions as applying to the extremity, not to a vein.

strategies: Apply the exclusion to the whole limb
Let therapy duration drive the device

steps.detail: Mastectomy with node dissection on the left, fistula on the right.
Nothing appropriate in either upper extremity.
Long-term antibiotics already point toward a central device.

elimination.verdict: Consult for central vascular access.

questions.stem: A nurse has scrubbed the insertion site with chlorhexidine using friction for 30 seconds. Which action next would require the nurse to repeat the skin preparation?

options.text: Applying the tourniquet above the site before cleansing
options.rationale: The tourniquet distends the vein to make it visible and palpable. Ask: was it applied before or after antisepsis? Before, which is the correct order and does not touch the prepared skin.

options.text: Choosing a 20 gauge catheter for the planned infusion
options.rationale: Twenty gauge is the standard adult size, suitable for most medications and fluids. Ask: does catheter selection affect the sterility of the field? No. This is a reasonable decision about a different part of the procedure.

options.text: Palpating the vein once more to confirm its position before inserting
options.rationale: Repalpation means touching the cleansed skin with an unsterile finger. Ask: what does that do to the prepared field? It recontaminates it with skin flora from the nurse's hand and negates the antisepsis, which raises the risk of catheter-related infection. Vein position is confirmed before the prep, not after.

options.text: Waiting for the antiseptic to dry completely before inserting the catheter
options.rationale: Complete air drying is what allows the antiseptic to exert its full antimicrobial effect. Ask: does waiting harm the prep? No, it completes it. This is the required step, not an error.

questions.takeaway: The prep is only as good as what happens after it. Drying completely and not touching the site are the two steps that preserve the work the scrub did.
questions.strategy: One option describes touching the prepared skin and three do not. Ask what each action contacts.

strategies: Ask what the action touches
Identify the required steps and set them aside

steps.detail: Full air drying and applying the tourniquet before cleansing are both correct.
Only one option puts a finger back on the cleansed site.
Unsterile contact returns skin flora and negates the prep.

elimination.verdict: Repalpating the vein after antisepsis.

questions.stem: A patient has a midline catheter placed for a 10-day course of intravenous antibiotics. Which new prescription does the nurse question?

options.text: 0.9% sodium chloride at 75 mL/hr
options.rationale: Normal saline is isotonic at 308 mOsm/L. Ask: is hydration therapy an appropriate midline use? Yes, it is one of the named indications.

options.text: Parenteral nutrition at 60 mL/hr
options.rationale: Parenteral nutrition is a highly concentrated solution of dextrose, amino acids, lipids, vitamins, and trace elements. Ask: where does a midline tip end? Below the axilla, in peripheral circulation. Parenteral nutrition is explicitly excluded from midline use and requires central access, because its osmolarity far exceeds the peripheral limit and would damage the vein.

options.text: Morphine sulfate 2 mg intravenously every 4 hours as needed
options.rationale: Morphine is an analgesic and is not a vesicant. Ask: does it fall inside the midline's permitted use? Yes. Analgesics are listed among the appropriate therapies.

options.text: Cefazolin 1 g intravenously every 8 hours
options.rationale: An antibiotic is a non-vesicant medication with an osmolarity well within peripheral limits. Ask: is this within the stated use for a midline? Yes. Antibiotics, analgesics, and hydration therapy are the listed indications.

questions.takeaway: A midline is a long peripheral catheter, not a central line. Its tip ends below the axilla, so it obeys peripheral rules no matter how far up the arm it was inserted.
questions.strategy: Three prescriptions are ordinary infusions. Ask which one requires a tip in central circulation.

strategies: Ask where the tip ends
Check each order against the exclusion list

steps.detail: Below the axilla, so peripheral circulation.
No vesicants, no parenteral nutrition, no continuous vasopressors.
Antibiotic, saline, and analgesic are all permitted.

elimination.verdict: Parenteral nutrition.

questions.stem: A peripherally inserted central catheter has just been placed in a patient's right basilic vein. The catheter flushes easily and there is good blood return. Which action does the nurse take before starting the prescribed infusion?

options.text: Confirm placement by the presence of brisk blood return on aspiration
options.rationale: Blood return shows the lumen sits within a vessel and is not occluded. Ask: does it say which vessel, or how far the tip advanced? No. A catheter with its tip in a vein short of the superior vena cava still yields blood return, and those positions carry higher thrombosis rates.

options.text: Obtain chest radiography to confirm tip placement
options.rationale: Tip confirmation establishes that the catheter ends where it is supposed to, in the lower superior vena cava. Ask: what does easy flushing prove? Only that the lumen is open. A catheter can be patent and still be malpositioned, which is why x-ray confirmation of tip placement is required before use rather than optional.

options.text: Measure the external catheter length and compare it with the insertion record
options.rationale: Measuring the external segment detects migration over time by comparison with a baseline. Ask: is there a baseline yet, and does length locate the tip? There is no prior measurement, and length does not confirm position inside the chest.

options.text: Begin the infusion at a reduced rate and observe the site for 30 minutes
options.rationale: Starting slowly and observing is a reasonable precaution with peripheral infusions. Ask: does it substitute for knowing where the tip is? No. It begins the therapy before the required confirmation and puts the patient at risk of an infusion into the wrong location.

questions.takeaway: Patency and position are different questions. A PICC can flush, draw back, and still be in the wrong place, which is why radiographic confirmation is required before first use.
questions.strategy: Three options gather information that seems reassuring. Ask what each one actually proves about where the tip is.

strategies: Separate patency from position
Ask what the evidence proves

steps.detail: The location of the tip.
Flushing and blood return prove the lumen is open, not where it ends.
Observation during infusion is not confirmation before infusion.

elimination.verdict: Chest radiography before first use.

questions.stem: A patient is being discharged with a peripherally inserted central catheter in the left arm. Which statement by the patient indicates a correct understanding of the teaching?

options.text: I will have my blood pressure taken in my right arm from now on
options.rationale: Blood pressure measurement compresses the limb under the cuff. Ask: what does that do to a catheter running up that arm? It compresses the vessel and the catheter, risking damage and occlusion. Blood pressure cuffs and venipuncture are both avoided on the PICC arm, so moving them to the other side is the correct understanding.

options.text: If the line feels blocked I should push a little harder on the syringe to clear it
options.rationale: Resistance during flushing means something is obstructing the lumen. Ask: what does added pressure do to an obstructed catheter? It can rupture it or dislodge a clot into the circulation. The instruction is to stop and not use the line if resistance is felt.

options.text: I should change the dressing whenever I remember, about once a month
options.rationale: The dressing keeps the exit site clean, dry, and intact. Ask: how often is it changed? Every 5 to 7 days, and immediately if it becomes wet or soiled. A monthly interval leaves the site unprotected for weeks, and monthly flushing belongs to an implanted port rather than a PICC.

options.text: I can take a bath as long as I change the dressing afterward
options.rationale: Submerging the arm puts the exit site under water regardless of what follows. Ask: does a later dressing change undo the exposure? No. Baths and swimming are avoided entirely, and showering is done with a waterproof cover over the site.

questions.takeaway: The PICC arm is off limits for blood pressure cuffs and venipuncture, and the site stays dry. Resistance on flushing is a stop signal, not something to push through.
questions.strategy: Three statements describe a reasonable-sounding routine. Check each against a specific instruction rather than against whether it sounds careful.

strategies: Test each statement against a stated rule
Watch for the plausible routine

steps.detail: No blood pressure cuffs and no venipuncture on that side.
No submerging; shower with a waterproof cover.
Never force against resistance; dressing every 5 to 7 days.

elimination.verdict: Blood pressure in the other arm.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses an intravenous site and finds the surrounding skin is cool and pale with moderate swelling. The drip rate has slowed and no blood return is obtained. Which complication has occurred?

options.text: Hematoma
options.rationale: A hematoma is blood leaking into tissue at the insertion site, producing bruising, swelling, and tenderness. Ask: does the stem describe bruising? No, it describes pallor. Swelling is shared between the two, which is what makes this worth checking rather than dismissing.

options.text: Thrombosis
options.rationale: Thrombosis is a clot forming in or around the catheter, producing a swollen, painful limb and a decreased flow rate. Ask: which findings does it fail to explain? Cool, pale skin and absent blood return at the site. A clot slows flow, and it does not push fluid into the tissue.

options.text: Infiltration
options.rationale: Infiltration is IV fluid leaking out of the vein into the surrounding tissue. Ask: do the findings match? Exactly. Fluid sitting in the interstitium makes the skin cool and pale and produces edema, the catheter is no longer in the vessel so there is no blood return, and the resistance of the tissue slows the drip rate.

options.text: Phlebitis
options.rationale: Phlebitis is inflammation of the vein wall itself, producing pain, redness, warmth, a streak along the vein, and a palpable cord. Ask: is this site warm or cool? Cool. Inflammation raises local temperature, so a cool site points away from phlebitis even though both complications look alarming.

questions.takeaway: Cool and pale means fluid has left the vein. Warm and red with a cord means the vein wall is inflamed. Both begin with stopping the infusion and removing the catheter.
questions.strategy: Two options produce swelling and two produce a slowed drip. Use skin temperature and blood return to separate them.

strategies: Read skin temperature first
Ask what each complication explains

steps.detail: Cool rules out the inflammatory picture.
Absent return means the catheter is not in the vessel.
Bruising is absent, and a clot does not move fluid into tissue.

elimination.verdict: Infiltration.

questions.stem: While a nurse is changing the injection cap on a patient's central venous catheter, the patient suddenly reports chest pain and severe shortness of breath. The blood pressure falls to 84 over 48 and a churning murmur is audible over the precordium. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Administer 100 percent oxygen by nonrebreather mask
options.rationale: High-flow oxygen improves saturation and helps the trapped air be reabsorbed. Ask: does it address the source? No. It is part of the response and it does not stop air from entering.

options.text: Clamp the catheter tubing
options.rationale: Clamping closes the pathway between room air and the venous system. Ask: what is still happening while anything else is done? Air continues to enter. Stopping the source is the first action because every additional second adds volume to the embolus, and the remaining steps treat what has already entered.

options.text: Activate the rapid response team
options.rationale: A rapid response brings additional expertise to the bedside. Ask: can the nurse stop the entry of air faster than a team can arrive? Yes, by reaching for the clamp. Calling is essential and it is not the first action when a one-second intervention stops the cause.

options.text: Position the patient in left lateral Trendelenburg
options.rationale: Left lateral Trendelenburg traps air in the right atrium away from the pulmonary outflow tract so it cannot be pumped into the lungs. Ask: is it necessary? Yes, and it comes immediately after clamping. It manages the air already inside while clamping prevents more.

questions.takeaway: Sudden dyspnea, chest pain, hypotension, and a mill-wheel murmur during line manipulation is air embolism. Clamp, position in left lateral Trendelenburg, call rapid response, and give 100 percent oxygen.
questions.strategy: All four actions belong to this emergency. The question is sequence, and the first action is the one that stops the cause rather than treats the effect.

strategies: Stop the source before treating the effect
Sequence actions that are all correct

steps.detail: Air entering during a cap change produces this exact picture.
Air keeps entering until the tubing is clamped.
Position, call, oxygen all follow.

elimination.verdict: Clamp the tubing.

questions.stem: For each patient situation, indicate the vascular access device the nurse anticipates.

rows.text: Needs a single dose of intravenous antiemetic in the emergency department and is expected to go home the same day
rows.rationale: A short peripheral catheter is the standard device for short-term therapy with isotonic or mildly hypertonic solutions. Ask: how long is access needed, and is the solution irritating? Hours, and no. Nothing about this situation calls for a longer or deeper device.

rows.text: Needs 10 days of intravenous antibiotics and has poor forearm veins that will not sustain repeated short catheters
rows.rationale: A midline is 3 to 8 inches, placed in the upper arm with its tip below the axilla, and dwells up to 4 weeks. Ask: is the therapy non-vesicant and within the peripheral osmolarity limit? Antibiotics are, and 10 days exceeds what a short catheter should carry. Midlines are indicated for antibiotics, analgesics, and hydration.

rows.text: Requires parenteral nutrition at home for the next several weeks after bowel surgery
rows.rationale: Parenteral nutrition is highly concentrated and requires a tip in central circulation. Ask: which device gives central access for weeks to months? A PICC, whose tip sits in the lower superior vena cava and which is specifically indicated for parenteral nutrition, vesicants, and irritating medications.

rows.text: Will receive chemotherapy every three weeks for the next year and wants to continue swimming between cycles
rows.rationale: An implanted port is a subcutaneous reservoir with no external catheter, accessed with a non-coring needle and flushed monthly when not in use. Ask: what does the intermittent schedule and the swimming both point to? A device with nothing outside the skin. It also carries the lowest infection risk of the central devices.

rows.text: Has end-stage kidney disease and needs immediate access for treatment while a fistula matures
rows.rationale: A hemodialysis catheter is large bore at 11 to 14 French to allow the rapid blood withdrawal and return that dialysis requires. Ask: can another central device do this work? No. It is dedicated to dialysis, never used for routine infusion or blood draws, and managed by dialysis-trained staff.

rows.text: Needs a continuous vasopressor infusion titrated in the intensive care unit and already has a central catheter in the internal jugular vein
rows.rationale: This row is the trap in the set. Vasopressors are vesicants and require central access, and the patient already has a nontunneled central catheter, so the question is what the nurse anticipates if that line must be replaced for ongoing therapy. A PICC provides central access for weeks to months with far lower infection risk than a nontunneled catheter, which carries the highest infection risk of the central devices and is intended for days to weeks.

questions.takeaway: Device selection runs on four criteria: therapy duration, solution osmolarity, vein condition, and patient diagnosis and preference. Duration sets the family of devices and the solution decides whether the tip must be central.
questions.strategy: Two rows share an answer. Ask duration first, then whether the solution can go peripherally, and the device usually names itself.

strategies: Ask duration, then osmolarity
Watch for the repeat

steps.detail: Hours, days to weeks, weeks to months, a year, ongoing dialysis.

steps.action: Ask whether the tip must be central
steps.detail: Parenteral nutrition, chemotherapy, and vasopressors all say yes.
Two different situations both call for central access over weeks to months.

elimination.verdict: Short peripheral, midline, PICC, port, dialysis catheter, PICC.

questions.nursesNote: 1400: Patient admitted for dehydration after three days of poor oral intake. Prescribed 0.9% sodium chloride at 150 mL per hour. Access is a 22 gauge catheter in the left forearm, placed on the first attempt. 1600: Patient is oriented to person, place, and time and reports feeling steadier. Lungs clear to auscultation bilaterally. Heart rate 84, blood pressure 128 over 76, respirations 16, oxygen saturation 97 percent on room air. Urine output 60 mL over the past hour. 1900: Patient asks the same question about the time three times in ten minutes. Respirations 26 and shallow. Fine crackles audible at both lung bases. Oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air. Heart rate 104. Blood pressure 152 over 88. Skin at the IV site is intact with good blood return and no redness.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings at 1900 that require the nurse to intervene.

segments.text: Patient asks the same question about the time three times in ten minutes
segments.rationale: New confusion is a change in mental status from a documented baseline. Ask: was this patient oriented earlier? Yes, fully at 1600. Confusion is one of the three findings to assess frequently in an older adult receiving fluids, and it is the one most often attributed to age or to the hospital instead of to the volume being infused.

segments.text: Respirations 26 and shallow
segments.rationale: Tachypnea is a respiratory rate above normal. Ask: what has changed? The rate rose from 16 to 26 in three hours with no new respiratory diagnosis. Dyspnea is a listed sign of fluid overload, and rapid shallow breathing is how it presents before the patient reports it.

segments.text: Fine crackles audible at both lung bases
segments.rationale: Crackles are the sound of fluid in the small airways. Ask: were the lungs clear before? Yes, at 1600. Crackles are the third of the three findings named for frequent assessment in this population, and new bibasilar crackles during an infusion is pulmonary edema until proven otherwise.

segments.text: Oxygen saturation 90 percent on room air
segments.rationale: Oxygen saturation measures how much hemoglobin is carrying oxygen. Ask: is a drop from 97 to 90 explained by anything else in the note? No. Fluid in the alveoli interferes with gas exchange, which is the mechanism connecting this value to the crackles.

segments.text: Heart rate 104
segments.rationale: Tachycardia is a heart rate above 100. Ask: does this finding alone require intervention, or is it part of the picture the others already establish? It is a mild rise from 84 and is nonspecific on its own. It supports the assessment and does not independently demand action.

segments.text: Blood pressure 152 over 88
segments.rationale: A rising blood pressure can accompany volume expansion. Ask: does this value require intervention by itself? No. It is elevated and not dangerous, and the note gives no prior hypertension history to compare it against.

segments.text: Skin at the IV site is intact with good blood return and no redness
segments.rationale: Blood return and intact skin indicate the catheter is within the vessel and the site is uninflamed. Ask: does this describe a problem? No, it rules two out. Infiltration and phlebitis are both excluded, which is what tells you the problem is systemic rather than local.

segments.text: Urine output 60 mL over the past hour
segments.rationale: Urine output reflects renal perfusion and fluid handling. Ask: is 60 mL in an hour adequate? Yes, comfortably above the usual 30 mL per hour threshold. This value was recorded at 1600 and is not a 1900 finding.

questions.takeaway: Confusion, dyspnea, and crackles are one finding wearing three coats in an older patient receiving fluids. All three are early fluid overload, and confusion is the one that gets blamed on something else.
questions.strategy: Several findings changed between 1600 and 1900 and several did not. Compare each 1900 value against its own earlier value before deciding whether it requires action.

strategies: Compare each value with its own baseline
Separate supporting findings from acting findings

steps.detail: Orientation, respiratory rate, breath sounds, and saturation all moved.
Every one of those is a sign of volume the patient cannot handle.
Heart rate and blood pressure support the picture, the site findings exclude a local problem, and the output was recorded earlier.

elimination.verdict: New confusion, tachypnea, bibasilar crackles, and the falling saturation.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A patient receiving intravenous vancomycin through a forearm catheter reports burning at the site. The nurse finds redness extending along the line of the vein, warmth, and a firm cord that can be palpated for about half an inch. There is blood return and no swelling.

These findings indicate [[1]].

The nurse's first action is to [[2]].

The most likely cause in this patient is [[3]].

options.text: infiltration
options.rationale: Infiltration is fluid leaking into surrounding tissue, producing cool pale skin, edema, a slowed drip, and no blood return. Ask: which of those appear here? None. Blood return is present and there is no swelling, so the fluid has not left the vein.

options.text: phlebitis
options.rationale: Phlebitis is inflammation of the vein wall. Ask: do the findings match? Redness along the vein, warmth, and a palpable cord are the defining signs, and the presence of blood return with no swelling tells you the catheter is still in the vessel.

options.text: a hematoma
options.rationale: A hematoma is blood collecting in tissue at the insertion site, producing bruising, swelling, and tenderness. Ask: does the stem describe bruising along a vein, or redness along it? Redness, and there is no swelling.

options.text: a catheter-related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: A CRBSI is a systemic infection with fever, chills, hypotension, and altered mental status and no other identifiable source. Ask: does the stem give any systemic finding? No, everything described is local to the site and the vein.

options.text: apply a cold compress and continue the infusion
options.rationale: Cold reduces local blood flow and can ease discomfort. Ask: is comfort the goal while the cause remains in place? No, and a warm moist compress rather than cold is what the intervention for phlebitis specifies.

options.text: flush the catheter with normal saline to test patency
options.rationale: Flushing checks whether the lumen is open. Ask: is patency in question? No. Blood return is already present, so flushing adds volume to an inflamed vein and delays removal.

options.text: stop the infusion and remove the catheter
options.rationale: Stopping ends the exposure and removing the catheter takes out the object inflaming the vein. Ask: what does the intervention list specify? Stop the infusion, remove the catheter, apply a warm moist compress, notify the provider, and document the grade. Nothing useful happens while the catheter stays in an inflamed vein.

options.text: slow the infusion and reassess in one hour
options.rationale: Slowing reduces the rate at which an irritating drug reaches the vein. Ask: does it stop the irritation? No, it prolongs it. The intervention for phlebitis is to stop, not to moderate.

options.text: mechanical irritation from catheter movement
options.rationale: Mechanical phlebitis results from the catheter moving within the vein, usually from an oversized catheter or an unsecured one at a point of flexion. Ask: does the stem point to movement or to the infusate? To the drug. This is a real type of phlebitis and it is not what this stem describes.

options.text: bacterial contamination from poor aseptic technique
options.rationale: Bacterial phlebitis follows a break in asepsis and tends to appear with systemic signs or purulent drainage at grade 4. Ask: does the stem report drainage or fever? Neither. It is one of the three types and the stem gives no evidence for it.

options.text: an allergic reaction to the medication
options.rationale: An allergic reaction produces urticaria, itching, bronchospasm, or hypotension and is systemic rather than confined to one vein. Ask: is the redness spread over the body or tracking along a single vessel? Along the vein, which is inflammation rather than hypersensitivity.

options.text: chemical irritation from the infused medication
options.rationale: Chemical phlebitis is inflammation caused by an irritating solution. Ask: what is running? Vancomycin, a venous irritant with a pH below 5 that causes phlebitis during peripheral infusion. The drug named in the stem is the evidence that selects this type.

questions.takeaway: Phlebitis has three types and they are separated by the history, not by the appearance. Mechanical is about the catheter, chemical is about the solution, bacterial is about technique.
questions.strategy: The drug named in the stem is not decoration. Vancomycin is a venous irritant, and naming it is how the question tells you which of the three types applies.

strategies: Use blood return to locate the problem
Let the named drug select the type

steps.detail: Blood return present and no swelling means the fluid is still in the vein.
Redness along the vein, warmth, and a palpable cord.
An irritating drug points to the chemical type.

elimination.verdict: Phlebitis; stop and remove the catheter; chemical irritation from the drug.

questions.scenario: A patient with a nontunneled central venous catheter in the subclavian vein has been receiving intravenous antibiotics for four days. Over the past two hours the patient has become confused and is shaking with chills. Temperature is 39.1 C, heart rate 126, blood pressure 86 over 48, respirations 24, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. The catheter exit site is clean and dry with no redness or drainage. The lungs are clear, the urine is clear and pale, and the abdomen is soft and nontender. The patient has no cough, no wound, and no other invasive devices.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Remove the dressing and repalpate the site to check for tenderness
options.rationale: Repalpating a central line site with unsterile fingers contaminates it. Ask: does the assessment already answer the question? Yes, the site is clean and dry with no drainage. This adds risk without adding information.

options.text: Apply a warm compress to the catheter exit site
options.rationale: Warm compresses are used for phlebitis at a peripheral site. Ask: does the stem describe local inflammation? No, the exit site is clean and dry. This treats a finding that is not present.

options.text: Slow the antibiotic infusion and recheck the temperature in one hour
options.rationale: Slowing an infusion is a response to speed shock or to an infusion reaction. Ask: do the findings fit a rate problem? No. Delaying an hour in a hypotensive, febrile patient forfeits the time in which cultures and treatment matter most.

options.text: Notify the provider and prepare for possible catheter removal
options.rationale: Removal eliminates the source when the catheter is the origin of the infection. Ask: what does the treatment list specify? Blood cultures, intravenous antibiotics, and removal of the catheter if needed. The nontunneled catheter carries the highest infection risk of the central devices and is the only plausible source here.

options.text: Obtain two sets of blood cultures before antibiotics are changed
options.rationale: Blood cultures identify the organism in the bloodstream and the paired sets help establish whether the catheter is the source. Ask: why before new antibiotics? Because once the drug is in, the organism may not grow, and the identification determines the treatment.

options.text: Catheter thrombosis
options.rationale: Thrombosis is a clot in or around the catheter, producing a swollen painful limb and a decreased flow rate. Ask: does the stem report either? Neither. It also does not produce fever with rigors.

options.text: Speed shock
options.rationale: Speed shock is a drug reaching a toxic concentration because it entered too quickly, producing flushing, headache, chest tightness, and shock. Ask: does the stem describe a rate problem or a fever? Fever and rigors, which speed shock does not cause.

options.text: Catheter-related bloodstream infection
options.rationale: A CRBSI is a bloodstream infection caused by the catheter, presenting with fever, chills, hypotension, and altered mental status and no other identifiable source. Ask: does the stem exclude other sources? Deliberately. Clear lungs, clear urine, soft abdomen, no cough, no wound, and no other devices leave the four-day central line as the source.

options.text: Air embolism
options.rationale: Air embolism follows air entering the venous system, producing sudden dyspnea, chest pain, a mill-wheel murmur, and hypotension. Ask: is the onset sudden and respiratory? No, it developed over two hours with fever and chills.

options.text: Blood pressure response to treatment
options.rationale: Blood pressure reflects perfusion, and 86 over 48 is the finding that makes this urgent rather than merely concerning. Ask: what would improvement look like? A rising pressure as the systemic response is controlled.

options.text: Temperature trend over the next several hours
options.rationale: Temperature reflects the systemic inflammatory response to the infection. Ask: does it measure the problem being treated? Directly, and a falling temperature after cultures and treatment is the expected response.

options.text: Whether the patient reports pain at the insertion site
options.rationale: Site pain is a local symptom. Ask: does its absence or presence tell you whether the systemic infection is resolving? No, and the stem already establishes the site is unremarkable.

options.text: Volume of antibiotic infused per hour
options.rationale: Infusion volume records what was delivered. Ask: does it measure the patient's response? No, it measures the nurse's task completion.

options.text: Appearance of the catheter exit site over the next 24 hours
options.rationale: Exit site appearance detects local infection. Ask: is the site the problem here? No, it is already clean and dry. A bloodstream infection can occur with a normal-looking site, so watching it measures the wrong thing.

questions.takeaway: A catheter-related bloodstream infection is diagnosed partly by exclusion, and a clean exit site does not rule it out. Dwell time is a primary risk factor, which is why line necessity is reviewed daily.
questions.strategy: The stem spends several clauses ruling things out. Those negatives are the evidence, not filler, and they are what leave the catheter as the only source.

strategies: Read the negatives as evidence
Match the parameter to the problem, not to the device

steps.detail: Clear lungs, clear urine, soft abdomen, no cough, no wound, no other devices.
A four-day nontunneled central catheter, the device with the highest infection risk.
Temperature and blood pressure track the infection; the site appearance does not.

elimination.verdict: Cultures and possible removal; catheter-related bloodstream infection; temperature and blood pressure.
